questions.title: One six is enough
questions.prompt: Roll two independent fair six-sided dice. What is the probability that at least one is a six?
hints: Count the complement.
Neither die is a six with probability \(\left(\frac56\right)^2\).
questions.solution: The complement has probability \(\frac{25}{36}\). Subtract it from 1 to obtain \(\frac{11}{36}\). Adding \(\frac{1}{6}\) + \(\frac{1}{6}\) counts the double-six outcome twice.
questions.followup: Now roll n dice. How many are needed to make the probability exceed 90%?
questions.followSolution: Require \(\left(\frac56\right)^n<0.1\). Taking logs gives \(n>12.63\), so 13 dice.

questions.title: A sum changes the sample space
questions.prompt: Two fair dice have sum 8. Given this information, what is the probability that their values are equal?
hints: List ordered pairs with sum 8.
There are five possible ordered pairs.
questions.solution: The conditional sample space is (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2). Only (4,4) is a double, so the answer is \(\frac{1}{5}\). Independence before conditioning does not imply independence after it.
questions.followup: What is the conditional mean of the first die?
questions.followSolution: By symmetry the two conditional means are equal and sum to 8, so each is 4.

questions.title: Learn which coin you picked
questions.prompt: Choose with equal probability between a fair coin and a coin that always lands heads. You flip the chosen coin once and see heads. What is the probability it is the always-heads coin?
hints: Write the likelihood under each coin.
The joint probabilities of selection and a head are \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\).
questions.solution: The always-heads branch contributes \(\frac{1}{2}\) to the probability of heads. The fair branch contributes \(\frac{1}{4}\). Normalising gives \(\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\frac23\). The posterior is not the prior \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.followup: After k consecutive heads, derive the posterior.
questions.followSolution: It is \(\frac{1}{1+2^{-k}}\). One tail rules out the always-heads coin entirely.

questions.title: A promising signal with a low base rate
questions.prompt: Only 2% of candidate signals are genuinely useful. A test passes a useful signal with probability 90% and a useless one with probability 10%. Given a pass, what is the probability the signal is useful?
hints: Use base rates as well as test accuracy.
The two pass masses are \(0.02\times0.9\) and \(0.98\times0.1\).
questions.solution: \[P(\text{useful}\mid\text{pass})=\frac{0.018}{0.018+0.098}=\frac9{58}\approx0.15517.\] High sensitivity does not compensate for many false passes from the large useless population. This calculation assumes the stated base rate and test characteristics apply to the candidate pool.
questions.followup: If you independently run the test twice and both pass, what changes?
questions.followSolution: Under conditional independence given usefulness, the posterior is \[\frac{0.02\times0.9^2}{0.02\times0.9^2+0.98\times0.1^2}=\frac{81}{130}\approx0.62308.\] Independence is a substantive assumption.

questions.title: Without replacement
questions.prompt: An urn contains 6 red and 4 blue balls. Draw two uniformly without replacement. What is the probability that their colours differ?
hints: Count red-blue unordered pairs.
There are \(6\times4\) favourable pairs and \(\binom{10}{2}\) total pairs.
questions.solution: There are 24 mixed-colour pairs out of 45 possible pairs, giving \(\frac{8}{15}\). Alternatively sum \(\frac6{10}\frac49+\frac4{10}\frac69\). Replacement would change the second denominator.
questions.followup: Generalise to r red and b blue.
questions.followSolution: The probability is \(\frac{2rb}{(r+b)(r+b-1)}\).

questions.title: Overlapping heads
questions.prompt: Flip a fair coin 20 times. Count adjacent HH pairs, allowing overlaps (HHH contains two pairs). What is the expected count?
hints: Create an indicator for each adjacent position.
Independence between the indicators is unnecessary for the mean.
questions.solution: There are 19 adjacent positions. Each indicator has expectation \(\frac{1}{4}\), so linearity gives \(\frac{19}{4}=4.75\). The indicators overlap, but linearity of expectation still holds.
questions.followup: For n flips, derive the variance of the count.
questions.followSolution: For \(n\geq2\), each indicator has variance \(\frac{3}{16}\); adjacent indicators have covariance \(\frac18-\frac1{16}=\frac1{16}\) and disjoint ones have covariance zero. The variance is \(\frac{3(n-1)+2(n-2)}{16}=\frac{5n-7}{16}\).

questions.title: The larger die
questions.prompt: Roll two independent fair six-sided dice. What is the expected maximum?
hints: Use \(P(\max=k)\), or a tail sum.
\(P(\max\leq k)=\frac{k^2}{36}\).
questions.solution: \(P(\max=k)=\frac{k^2-(k-1)^2}{36}=\frac{2k-1}{36}\). Sum \(\frac{k(2k-1)}{36}\) from 1 to 6 to get \(\frac{161}{36}\approx4.47222\). A maximum is not the maximum of the means.
questions.followup: What is the expected minimum?
questions.followSolution: max+min equals the sum pointwise. Thus \(\mathbb E[\min]=7-\frac{161}{36}=\frac{91}{36}\).

questions.title: The first uniform point
questions.prompt: Draw three independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) values. What is the expected minimum?
hints: Integrate the survival function.
\(P(\min>x)=(1-x)^3\) for \(0\leq x\leq1\).
questions.solution: For a nonnegative variable, \(\mathbb E[M]=\int P(M>x)\,dx\). Here \(\int_0^1(1-x)^3\,dx=\frac14\). In general the minimum of n independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) values has mean \(\frac{1}{n+1}\).
questions.followup: Find \(\mathbb E[\max]\) and its CDF.
questions.followSolution: \(P(\max\leq x)=x^3\) on [0,1], and \(\mathbb E[\max]=\frac34\).

questions.title: Collect all four
questions.prompt: Each independent draw returns one of four equally likely symbols. How many draws do you expect before seeing all four?
hints: Split the wait into stages after each new symbol.
The success probabilities are 1, \(\frac{3}{4}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{1}{4}\).
questions.solution: The expected stage lengths are 1, \(\frac{4}{3}\), 2, 4. Their sum is \(\frac{25}{3}\). Geometric waiting times need not be identically distributed for their expectations to add.
questions.followup: Generalise to m equally likely symbols.
questions.followSolution: The mean is \(m\left(1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1m\right)\). Unequal probabilities require a different argument; replacing them by their average is invalid.

questions.title: Wait for a head then a tail
questions.prompt: Flip a fair coin until the consecutive pattern HT appears. What is the expected number of flips?
hints: Track whether the latest flip was H.
Write one recurrence from the empty state and one from H.
questions.solution: Let \(E_0\) be the wait from no useful suffix and \(E_H\) from suffix H. \(E_0=1+\frac{E_0+E_H}{2}\) and \(E_H=1+\frac{E_H}{2}\). Thus \(E_H=2\) and \(E_0=4\). Repeated H leaves you in the H state.
questions.followup: Why does HH have a different wait?
questions.followSolution: For HH, \(E_H=1+\frac{E_0}{2}\). Solve with the same \(E_0\) equation to get \(E_0=6\). A tail destroys the partial match.

questions.title: Three heads in a row
questions.prompt: Flip a fair coin until HHH first appears. Find the expected total number of flips, including the final three.
hints: Use states with 0, 1 and 2 trailing heads.
A tail sends every nonterminal state to state 0.
questions.solution: The stated recurrences give \(E_1=E_0-2\) and \(E_2=1+\frac{E_0}{2}\). Substitution yields \(E_0-2=1+\frac{1+1.5E_0}{2}\), so \(E_0=14\). The shortcut \(\frac1{P(HHH)}=8\) treats overlapping trials as disjoint independent attempts.
questions.followup: Generalise to k heads with head probability p.
questions.followSolution: The expected wait is \(\frac{1-p^k}{(1-p)p^k}\) for \(0<p<1\). At \(p=1\) it is k by continuity.

questions.title: Exit a fair random walk
questions.prompt: A simple symmetric random walk starts at 5 on the integers and stops on first hitting 0 or 12. What is its expected stopping time?
hints: The mean solves \(t_i=1+\frac{t_{i-1}+t_{i+1}}2\).
Use boundary conditions \(t_0=t_{12}=0\).
Try a quadratic in i.
questions.solution: The solution is \(t_i=i(12-i)\): its second discrete difference is −2 and it is zero at the boundaries. Hence \(t_5=35\). The finite interval ensures finite expected exit time.
questions.followup: What is the probability of hitting 12 first?
questions.followSolution: Solve \(p_i=\frac{p_{i-1}+p_{i+1}}2\) with \(p_0=0,\quad p_{12}=1\). The answer is \(\frac{i}{12}\), hence \(\frac{5}{12}\).

questions.title: One reroll
questions.prompt: Roll a fair die and observe it. Either keep the value or discard it and roll once more, whose value you must accept. What is the optimal expected payoff?
hints: Compare each observed value with the mean of a fresh roll.
Keep 4, 5, 6; reroll 1, 2, 3.
questions.solution: The continuation value is 3.5. The expected optimum is \(\frac{3\times3.5+4+5+6}{6}=4.25\). The realised second roll can be worse, but the decision is based on conditional expectation.
questions.followup: If a reroll costs 1, what is the optimal value?
questions.followSolution: Continuation is 2.5. Reroll 1 and 2, keep 3 through 6. \(\text{Mean}=\frac{2\times2.5+3+4+5+6}{6}=\frac{23}{6}\).

questions.title: Three pieces, one triangle
questions.prompt: Choose two independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) cut locations on a unit stick. Cut at both. What is the probability the three lengths form a nondegenerate triangle?
hints: A triangle exists iff no piece is at least half the stick.
Order the cuts \(U<V\); the three pieces are \(U,\ V-U,\ 1-V\).
Measure the valid region inside \(0<U<V<1\).
questions.solution: The valid conditions are \(U<\frac12\), \(V>\frac12\) and \(V-U<\frac12\). Their region is a triangle of area \(\frac{1}{8}\) inside the ordered-cut triangle of area \(\frac{1}{2}\). The ratio is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Equality boundaries have probability zero.
questions.followup: Does sequentially choosing a piece uniformly and cutting it uniformly give the same answer?
questions.followSolution: No. It defines a different distribution over length triples. Specify the cutting procedure before using a geometric uniformity argument.

questions.title: A memoryless wait
questions.prompt: A waiting time is Exponential with rate \(\frac{1}{2}\) per minute. Given that you have already waited 3 minutes, what is the expected total waiting time in minutes?
hints: Distinguish total time from remaining time.
The expected remaining time is \(\frac1{\text{rate}}\).
questions.solution: Memorylessness gives \(\mathbb E[T-3\mid T>3]=2\). The expected total is \(3+2=5\). Memorylessness is specific to this model; an arbitrary wait distribution does not have it.

questions.title: Which clock rings first?
questions.prompt: Independent exponential clocks have rates 3 and 2. What is the probability that the rate-3 clock rings first?
hints: Integrate \(f_X(t)P(Y>t)\).
The integrand is \(3e^{-5t}\).
questions.solution: \(\int_0^\infty3e^{-3t}e^{-2t}\,dt=\frac35\). The minimum has rate 5. Ties have probability zero.
questions.followup: Are the winning clock and the time of the first ring independent?
questions.followSolution: Yes for independent exponential clocks with constant rates. The joint density of winner 1 and time t is \(3e^{-5t}\), which factors into \(\frac{3}{5}\) times \(5e^{-5t}\).

questions.title: Correlation survives averaging
questions.prompt: One hundred variables each have variance 1. Every distinct pair has correlation 0.1. What is the variance of their arithmetic mean?
hints: Expand the variance of a sum, including off-diagonal terms.
There are \(n(n-1)\) ordered covariance terms.
questions.solution: \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{n+n(n-1)\rho}{n^2}=\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{n}=0.109.\] The independence shortcut gives 0.01 and misses the common component.
questions.followup: What happens as n grows?
questions.followSolution: The variance tends to \(\rho=0.1\); averaging does not eliminate the common shock. Equicorrelation must also satisfy \(\rho\geq-\frac1{n-1}\).

questions.title: A hundred dependent observations
questions.prompt: A stationary AR(1) series has lag-one autocorrelation \(\rho=0.8\) and marginal variance \(\sigma^2\). Define effective sample size by equating the mean-estimation variance to \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n_{\mathrm{eff}}}\). Derive the large-sample approximation, then report \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\) for \(n=100\). Use the asymptotic result, not the finite-n tapered correction.
hints: The autocorrelation at lag k is \(\rho^k\).
The variance inflation factor is \(1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho^k=\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\).
questions.solution: The approximation gives \(\frac{100\times0.2}{1.8}=\frac{100}{9}\approx11.11\). This is an asymptotic mean-estimation comparison, not a universal effective sample size for every estimator.
questions.followup: Write the exact finite-n variance factor.
questions.followSolution: \[\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)}{\gamma_0/n}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)\rho^k.\] The taper matters in short samples or near unit roots.

questions.title: Measurement error shrinks a slope
questions.prompt: Let \(Y=2X+\varepsilon\). You observe \(W=X+u\). X,u,ε are mutually independent, centred, with \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(u)=3\). What is the population OLS slope of Y on W with an intercept?
hints: The slope is \(\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(W,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(W)}\).
The numerator is 2 and denominator 4.
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Cov}(W,Y)=2\operatorname{Var}(X)=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=1+3=4\), hence slope \(\frac{1}{2}\). Independent measurement error in the regressor attenuates the slope; error in the response alone would not.
questions.followup: What if u is correlated with ε?
questions.followSolution: The numerator gains \(\operatorname{Cov}(u,\varepsilon)\). The attenuation conclusion can fail, including sign reversal. Independence was doing real work.

questions.title: Three correlations must fit together
questions.prompt: Standardised variables X,Y,Z satisfy \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Corr}(Y,Z)=0.8\). What is the smallest possible \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z)\)?
hints: The correlation matrix must be positive semidefinite.
Let \[a=\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y),\quad b=\operatorname{Corr}(Y,Z),\quad c=\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z).\]
The determinant gives \((c-ab)^2\leq(1-a^2)(1-b^2)\).
questions.solution: The allowed interval is \(ab\pm\sqrt{(1-a^2)(1-b^2)}\). Here it is \(0.64\pm0.36\), so \(c\geq0.28\). Pairwise bounds \([-1,1]\) alone are insufficient. At the boundary the matrix is singular, and the bound is attainable.
questions.followup: Construct variables attaining the minimum.
questions.followSolution: Take independent standardised Y,U and set \(X=0.8Y+0.6U\), \(Z=0.8Y-0.6U\). Then \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z)=0.64-0.36=0.28\).

questions.title: Residuals sum to zero
questions.prompt: You fit OLS with an intercept. Explain why the residuals sum to zero, and why this need not hold without an intercept.
hints: Write the derivative of squared error with respect to the intercept.
Equivalently use \(X^{\mathsf T}r=0\).
questions.solution: At a least-squares optimum, differentiating \(\sum_i(y_i-a-b^{\mathsf T}x_i)^2\) with respect to a gives \(-2\sum_i r_i=0\). In matrix terms, residuals are orthogonal to every design column, including the all-ones intercept column. Without that column there is no such normal equation.
questions.followup: Does zero residual mean imply the model is unbiased out of sample?
questions.followSolution: No. It is an in-sample algebraic property. Misspecification, leakage or a changed distribution can produce arbitrarily biased future predictions.

questions.title: A reversal after pooling
questions.prompt: Can a treatment have a higher success rate in each of two groups but a lower success rate overall? Construct a numerical example and explain the mechanism.
hints: Use different group weights for treatment and control.
Place most treatment observations in the harder group.
questions.solution: Example: easy group treatment \(\frac{9}{10}\) versus control \(\frac{80}{100}\); hard group treatment \(\frac{20}{100}\) versus control \(\frac{1}{10}\). Treatment wins within each (\(90\%>80\%,\quad20\%>10\%\)), but overall treatment is \(\frac{29}{110}\approx26.4\%\) and control \(\frac{81}{110}\approx73.6\%\). Group composition confounds the pooled comparison.
questions.followup: Does adjusting for every available variable fix causal inference?
questions.followSolution: No. Conditioning on colliders can introduce bias, and unmeasured confounding remains possible. Adjustment needs a causal argument.

questions.title: Estimate the end of a uniform interval
questions.prompt: You observe \(n=4\) iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta)\) values. The sample maximum is 8. Multiply it by the appropriate factor to obtain an unbiased estimator of \(\theta\). What estimate do you get?
hints: \(\mathbb E[\max]=\frac{n\theta}{n+1}\).
Multiply by \(\frac{n+1}{n}\).
questions.solution: The maximum has CDF \(\left(\frac m\theta\right)^n\) on \([0,\theta]\) and mean \(\frac{n\theta}{n+1}\). The unbiased estimator is \(\frac{(n+1)\max}{n}\). At \(n=4,\quad\max=8\) it equals 10. The maximum itself is the MLE but is biased down.
questions.followup: Is unbiasedness alone enough to choose an estimator?
questions.followSolution: No. Compare mean squared error, variance, stability and loss function. An unbiased estimator can have higher risk than a biased one.

questions.title: The unbiased variance divisor
questions.prompt: For iid observations with finite variance \(\sigma^2\), explain why \(\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2\) is biased down, and derive the unbiased correction.
hints: Use \(\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X-\mu)^2\).
Take expectations and use \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\).
questions.solution: Use \(\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X-\mu)^2\). The expectation of the first term is \(n\sigma^2\) and that of the subtracted term is \(n\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2\), so the sum has expectation \((n-1)\sigma^2\). Dividing by \(n-1\) gives an unbiased estimator for n>1. Normality is not needed for this expectation identity.
questions.followup: What breaks for correlated data?
questions.followSolution: Var(X̄) is no longer \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\). The same identity holds, but the familiar divisor does not generally remove the bias.

questions.title: At least one false discovery
questions.prompt: You run 20 independent tests of true null hypotheses, each at level 5%. What is the probability of at least one rejection?
hints: Work with the complement.
Independence is explicitly assumed.
questions.solution: The probability of no rejection is \(0.95^{20}\). The complement is about 0.641514. A single-test error rate is not a familywise error rate. Dependence changes the exact calculation.
questions.followup: Give a threshold that controls familywise error at 5% without independence.
questions.followSolution: Bonferroni uses \(\frac{0.05}{20}=0.0025\) per test. The union bound gives control for arbitrary dependence, assuming valid individual p-values.

questions.title: A p-value is not a posterior
questions.prompt: A paper reports \(p=0.03\). Is there a 97% probability its hypothesis is true? Define the p-value precisely and identify the missing ingredients for a posterior probability.
hints: The conditioning is on the null model, not the observed data.
A posterior needs a prior and an alternative likelihood.
questions.solution: A p-value is the probability, under the specified null and test procedure, of a statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not \(P(\text{null}\mid\text{data})\). A posterior needs prior model probabilities and likelihoods under null and alternatives. Selection and multiple tests also affect interpretation.
questions.followup: Does a large p-value establish the null?
questions.followSolution: No. The test may have low power. Equivalence or noninferiority questions need their own margins and tests.

questions.title: Random folds on overlapping labels
questions.prompt: Every sample at time t predicts the return from t to t+5. A researcher randomly splits rows into train and test and gets excellent results. Diagnose at least three problems and design a replacement validation scheme.
hints: Think label intervals, temporal dependence and preprocessing.
A training label may include outcomes inside a test interval.
Separate model selection from the final performance estimate.
questions.solution: Random splitting can put overlapping label outcomes in both sets; it can train on regimes after the tested date; and full-sample preprocessing or tuning can leak test information. Use chronological walk-forward splits, purge training labels whose intervals touch test labels, fit transforms only within each training fold, and keep a final untouched holdout. An embargo can add a gap for further dependence, chosen from the information horizon.
questions.followup: Why is merely shuffling less aggressively insufficient?
questions.followSolution: It does not explicitly remove label overlap or enforce a deployment-time information set. Validation must correspond to what was knowable at prediction time.

questions.title: A fitted scaler leaks quietly
questions.prompt: You split chronologically but fit a normalisation transform on the entire series before training. Explain the leakage and give a correct pipeline.
hints: Preprocessing learns parameters too.
The test distribution has influenced the training representation.
questions.solution: The full-series mean and scale incorporate future test observations. Fit each transform on training data, apply it unchanged to validation/test, and repeat inside every model-selection fold. After selection, refit on permitted pre-holdout data only.
questions.followup: Is using a rolling normaliser always safe?
questions.followSolution: Only if each value uses data available then, with an appropriate shift. A centred window or same-time data unavailable at execution leaks.

questions.title: Minimum-variance combination
questions.prompt: Two unbiased independent estimates of the same mean have variances 1 and 4. Combine them as \(wX+(1-w)Y\). What weight w minimises variance?
hints: Minimise \(w^2+4(1-w)^2\).
Differentiate and solve.
questions.solution: The derivative is \(2w-8(1-w)=0\), yielding \(w=\frac45\). The resulting variance is 0.8. Greater weight goes to the more precise estimator. Independence and common target are required.
questions.followup: With covariance c, derive the weight.
questions.followSolution: \(w=\frac{v_Y-c}{v_X+v_Y-2c}\), provided the denominator is positive. The optimum can lie outside [0,1] if unrestricted weights are allowed.

questions.title: Ridge changes the geometry
questions.prompt: For objective \(\lVert y-X\beta\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert\beta\rVert^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), derive \(\hat\beta\). Explain what happens along a nearly singular direction of X.
hints: Differentiate the quadratic objective.
Diagonalise \(X^{\mathsf T}X\).
questions.solution: The normal equation is \((X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)\hat\beta=X^{\mathsf T}y\), so \[\hat\beta=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y.\] Along an eigenvector with eigenvalue d, the OLS coefficient is multiplied by \(\frac d{d+\lambda}\) when OLS is defined. Small-eigenvalue directions shrink most. Usually an intercept is excluded from the penalty.
questions.followup: Why standardise features before ridge?
questions.followSolution: The penalty is scale-dependent. A change of units changes relative shrinkage unless the feature scale or penalty is adjusted.

questions.title: A Sharpe ratio needs dependence assumptions
questions.prompt: Someone annualises a daily Sharpe by multiplying by \(\sqrt{252}\). Derive the rule for iid daily returns and explain why it may fail with autocorrelation.
hints: Compute the mean and variance of a 252-day sum.
Include all cross-covariances in the dependent case.
questions.solution: For iid excess returns with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), a k-day sum has mean \(k\mu\) and variance \(k\sigma^2\), giving \(\sqrt k\,\frac\mu\sigma\). With autocovariance \(\gamma_h\), variance is \(k\gamma_0+2\sum_{h=1}^{k-1}(k-h)\gamma_h\). Positive autocorrelation increases this denominator relative to the iid rule. The derivation uses summed returns; compounding and costs introduce additional distinctions.
questions.followup: Can a smooth equity curve be evidence against a strategy?
questions.followSolution: It can signal stale pricing or smoothing that hides dependence and risk. Investigate the construction before trusting a high annualised Sharpe.

questions.title: Fit the best of a thousand
questions.prompt: You choose the best of 1,000 models using one validation set, then report that model’s validation score as expected future performance. What is wrong, and how would you fix it?
hints: The validation set has become part of the fitting procedure.
Distinguish selection from estimation.
questions.solution: Selection favours models with positive validation noise. The winning score is optimistically biased even if every candidate was fitted only on training data. Use nested time-aware validation for selection and an untouched final test for estimation; record all trials and uncertainty. Retesting repeatedly on the final test turns it into another validation set.
questions.followup: What if the 1,000 models are strongly correlated?
questions.followSolution: The effective search is smaller than 1,000 independent trials, but selection bias remains. The independence formula cannot be imported without checking dependence.

questions.title: Predictable is not executable
questions.prompt: Your model predicts the next recorded trade price with high accuracy. Design the checks needed before claiming a tradable edge.
hints: A recorded price is not necessarily an executable price.
Define the timestamp and action your strategy could take.
Include spreads, fees, latency, inventory and capacity.
questions.solution: Specify the prediction timestamp, publication delays and available features. Rebuild labels from executable bid/ask prices after realistic latency. Compare to a persistence baseline. Audit time ordering, stale prices, leakage and survivorship. Include fees, spread crossing, impact, turnover, shorting constraints and capacity. Evaluate chronological holdouts and P&L under an explicit decision rule. Forecast accuracy alone does not establish profit.
questions.followup: Why might a highly accurate model lose money?
questions.followSolution: Small wins and rare large losses, adverse selection, or transaction costs can dominate. Accuracy ignores payoff sizes and action constraints.

questions.title: Explain a research failure
questions.prompt: A strategy works in one period and fails in the next. Give a structured diagnosis that distinguishes implementation error, overfitting, regime change and costs.
hints: Start with invariants and a minimal baseline.
Compare signal quality with execution economics separately.
questions.solution: First reconcile data, timestamps, universe, labels and positions, and reproduce the earlier period. Then audit trials, tuning and overlap for overfit. Evaluate feature/return distributions and subperiod stability for a regime change. Finally decompose gross versus net returns, turnover, spread, fees and impact. Multiple causes can coexist; a story alone does not identify one.
questions.followup: What evidence would falsify your preferred explanation?

questions.title: Three rolls and a quoted market
questions.prompt: A contract pays the sum of three independent fair dice. A dealer quotes bid 10 and ask 11. Ignoring costs and risk aversion, what is your fair value?
hints: Use linearity of expectation.
Each die has mean 3.5.
questions.solution: The fair value is \(3\times3.5=10.5\). Buying at 11 or selling at 10 each has expected loss 0.5 per unit, so there is no positive expected-value trade for an uninformed risk-neutral taker.
questions.followup: One die is revealed as 6. What is fair value now?
questions.followSolution: \(6+2\times3.5=13\). Buying at an unchanged ask of 11 has expected edge 2 per unit, before costs and constraints.

questions.title: The counterparty knows more
questions.prompt: A contract pays either 0 or 100 with equal prior probabilities. Your ask is 55. Independently of the payoff, a buyer is equally likely to be informed (buys only when \(\text{payoff}=100\)) or uninformed (always buys). Conditional on a buy, what is the expected payoff?
hints: Condition on who buys and the outcome.
A buy occurs with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) from informed and \(\frac{1}{2}\) from uninformed.
questions.solution: The event buy has mass \(\frac{3}{4}\). The joint mass buy and high payoff is \(\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\). Thus \(P(\text{high}\mid\text{buy})=\frac23\) and \(\text{conditional fair value}=\frac{200}{3}\). Selling at 55 loses expected value despite being above the prior mean 50.
questions.followup: At what ask do you break even on buys under this fixed behavioural model?
questions.followSolution: At \(\frac{200}{3}\). This assumes uninformed buyers buy regardless of the ask and informed buyers still buy in the high state; in realistic models behaviour depends on price.

questions.title: A risk budget for a repeated bet
questions.prompt: A repeated independent bet wins even money with probability 0.6. You stake fraction f of wealth each time. What f maximises expected log wealth growth?
hints: Maximise \(0.6\log(1+f)+0.4\log(1-f)\).
Set the derivative to zero.
questions.solution: The derivative is \(\frac{0.6}{1+f}-\frac{0.4}{1-f}\). Setting it to zero gives \(f=0.2\). The optimum depends on accurate probabilities and the repeated log-utility objective; it is not a universally appropriate real-money stake.
questions.followup: How does uncertainty in p change the decision?
questions.followSolution: Plug-in Kelly can overbet. Shrinking probabilities toward \(\frac{1}{2}\) or using a fraction of the estimated stake reduces sensitivity; dependence and tail losses require a different model.

questions.title: Do not double-count diversification
questions.prompt: Two returns each have variance 4 and correlation 0.5. What is the variance of an equal-weight portfolio?
hints: Covariance equals correlation times both standard deviations.
Use both off-diagonal terms.
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Cov}=0.5\times2\times2=2\). \[\text{Portfolio variance}=0.25\times4+0.25\times4+2\times0.25\times2=3.\] An average of marginal variances alone would miss diversification; assuming zero covariance would overstate it.
questions.followup: What if the correlation is −1?
questions.followSolution: The equal-weight portfolio has zero variance under the exact equal-volatility model. That perfect cancellation is fragile to estimated correlations and differing exposures.

questions.title: Gamma is not delta
questions.prompt: A portfolio has delta 0 and gamma 0.08. Under a small underlying move \(\Delta S=5\), ignoring time decay and higher-order terms, what is its approximate value change?
hints: Use the second-order Taylor term.
The gamma contribution has a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.solution: \[\Delta V\approx\delta\,\Delta S+\frac12\gamma(\Delta S)^2=0+0.5\times0.08\times25=1.\] Delta neutrality removes the first-order term locally, not all risk.
questions.followup: What happens for \(\Delta S=-5\)?
questions.followSolution: The same gamma contribution +1, within the approximation. Theta, volatility changes and rehedging costs are not included.

questions.title: A synthetic forward
questions.prompt: For European options on a non-dividend asset, same strike \(K=100\) and maturity \(T=1\), \(S=100\) and continuously compounded rate \(r=0\). What is \(C-P\)?
hints: Use put-call parity.
questions.solution: Put-call parity gives \(C-P=100-100=0\). A call minus a put has terminal payoff \(S_T-K\), equal to a forward payoff. European exercise and identical strike/maturity matter.
questions.followup: What changes with known dividend present value D?
questions.followSolution: \(C-P=S-D-Ke^{-rT}\). American exercise can prevent equality.

questions.title: A fair-looking auction
questions.prompt: You bid for an asset with unknown common value. Your estimate is unbiased before bidding. Why can winning make your estimate too high, and how should that enter your bid?
hints: Winning is a selection event.
The highest noisy estimate tends to have positive error.
questions.solution: In a common-value auction, winning usually means your estimate exceeded others. Conditional on winning, your estimation error can be positive even when the unconditional error has mean zero. Bid using \(\mathbb E[\text{value}\mid\text{your signal},\text{winning}]\) and the auction/payment rules, not the raw estimate. The adjustment depends on competitors and information structure.
questions.followup: Does this apply identically to private-value auctions?
questions.followSolution: No. If your own consumption value is private and known, rivals’ lower bids need not be bad news about that value. Strategic bid shading can still arise for other reasons.

questions.title: Two constraints, one quote
questions.prompt: Your inventory is already long. You can lower both your bid and ask by the same amount or widen your spread symmetrically. Explain how these actions differ, and what information you need to choose.
hints: A skew changes the quote centre.
A wider spread changes execution probabilities on both sides.
questions.solution: Lowering the centre encourages selling and discourages further buying, helping reduce long inventory. Symmetric widening reduces fills on both sides and may protect against information risk but need not resolve the position. Choose using fair value, inventory risk, flow sensitivity, adverse selection, horizon and limits. Exact optimal prices require a model.
questions.followup: Why can a profitable expected edge still violate a sensible policy?
questions.followSolution: Position limits, correlated exposures, capital, tail risk or liquidity can make the trade infeasible even with positive standalone expectation.

questions.title: An antithetic pair
questions.prompt: For \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), estimate \(\mathbb E[U^2]\) using the average of \(U^2\) and \((1-U)^2\). Derive whether its variance is smaller than the average of two independent squared uniforms.
hints: Compute \(\operatorname{Cov}(U^2,(1-U)^2)\).
\(\mathbb E[U^2(1-U)^2]=\frac1{30}\) and \(\mathbb E[U^2]=\frac13\).
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Var}(U^2)=\frac15-\frac19=\frac4{45}\). The covariance is \(\frac1{30}-\frac19=-\frac7{90}\). Pair-average variance is \(\frac12\left(\frac4{45}-\frac7{90}\right)=\frac1{180}\). The average of two independent \(U^2\) values has variance \(\frac{2}{45}\). The antithetic pair is unbiased and reduces variance eightfold.
questions.followup: Does antithetic sampling always reduce variance?
questions.followSolution: No. It needs a favourable covariance structure. For a function symmetric about \(\frac{1}{2}\), the paired observations are identical: their average has the variance of one draw, twice the variance of two independent draws.

questions.title: When a sample was available
questions.prompt: A feature is labelled with event time 10:00:00 but arrives at 10:00:02. A simulated trade acts at 10:00:01. Is joining the feature by event time valid? Design the join.
hints: Event time and availability time are different.
Your information set must respect receipt/publication delay.
questions.solution: It is invalid if the feature was unavailable until 10:00:02. Join on the most recent feature whose availability time is at or before the decision time, respecting any execution delay. Keep both event and availability timestamps and define tie rules. An as-of join on event time alone can manufacture a predictive edge.
questions.followup: When is an event-time join sufficient?
questions.followSolution: Only when event time also represents actual availability at the decision point, or a correctly modelled delay is applied. Document that assumption.

questions.title: The denominator is part of the answer
questions.prompt: A variable has variance 9. What is the variance after multiplying it by 2 and adding 7?
hints: Translations do not affect variance.
Scaling multiplies variance by the square of the scale.
questions.solution: \(\operatorname{Var}(2X+7)=4\operatorname{Var}(X)=36\). The standard deviation doubles; the variance quadruples.
questions.followup: What is \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,-2X+7)\) when \(\operatorname{Var}(X)>0\)?
questions.followSolution: It is −1. Linear translation preserves covariance and negative scaling reverses its sign.

questions.title: A biased coin, twice
questions.prompt: A Bernoulli success probability p has a \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\) prior. Observe 3 successes and 1 failure. What is the posterior mean of p?
hints: Add successes and failures to the Beta parameters.
The posterior is \(\operatorname{Beta}(5,3)\).
questions.solution: Conjugacy gives \(\operatorname{Beta}(2+3,2+1)=\operatorname{Beta}(5,3)\), with mean \(\frac{5}{8}\). The empirical rate \(\frac{3}{4}\) and posterior mean differ because the prior contributes information.
questions.followup: What is the predictive probability of success on the next trial?
questions.followSolution: It equals the posterior mean \(\frac{5}{8}\). This uses exchangeable Bernoulli observations with a common fixed p.

questions.title: Stop when you look good
questions.prompt: You repeatedly compute an ordinary fixed-sample 5% significance test and stop the first time it rejects. Why is the claimed 5% error rate invalid? Give two principled alternatives.
hints: The sampling and stopping plan is part of the test.
Repeated opportunities to reject inflate the chance of crossing.
questions.solution: A fixed-sample p-value is calibrated for its specified sample size and procedure. Repeated looks with a data-dependent stop change that procedure and can inflate type-I error. Precommit to the sample size and test, or use a valid sequential procedure such as alpha spending or an appropriate always-valid test. Do not claim every stopping rule is invalid; the test must match it.
questions.followup: Does a martingale automatically justify optional stopping?
questions.followSolution: No. Optional-stopping equalities require conditions such as bounded stopping times or suitable integrability. Ignoring those conditions causes classic paradoxes.

questions.title: Choose a control variate
questions.prompt: To estimate \(\mathbb E[Y]\), you use \(Z=Y-c(X-\mathbb E[X])\) where \(\mathbb E[X]\) is known. Derive the variance-minimising c and the residual variance, assuming \(\operatorname{Var}(X)>0\).
hints: Expand \(\operatorname{Var}(Y-cX)\).
Differentiate the quadratic in c.
questions.solution: \[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)+c^2\operatorname{Var}(X)-2c\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).\] The optimum is \(c^*=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\). Substitution gives \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\left(1-\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)^2\right)\). The estimator remains unbiased for fixed c; estimating c on the same sample can require care in a finite-sample unbiasedness claim.
questions.followup: How would you estimate c without that complication?
questions.followSolution: Estimate c on an independent pilot sample, then hold it fixed on the main Monte Carlo sample.

questions.title: Count events, keep the exposure
questions.prompt: Four independent exponential waiting times, with a common unknown rate λ > 0, are fully observed: 1, 2, 3 and 4 seconds. Derive the likelihood, verify its maximum, and report the maximum likelihood rate in events per second.
hints: An exponential density is λ exp(−λx) for x ≥ 0.
Sum the exposure times before differentiating the log-likelihood.
questions.solution: The joint density is λ^4 exp(−10λ), and the log-likelihood is 4 log λ − 10λ. Its derivative is 4/λ − 10, zero at λ = 0.4. The second derivative −4/λ² is negative, and the likelihood approaches zero at both limits. Thus this is the unique global maximum, in inverse seconds. The mean wait is 2.5 seconds; the rate is its reciprocal.
questions.followup: Now suppose only two events were observed over 10 seconds of total exposure, with the other waits independently right-censored. Derive the rate estimate. What changes if no events occur?
questions.followSolution: Each event supplies a density λ exp(−λx); each censored observation supplies survival exp(−λc). The likelihood is proportional to λ² exp(−10λ), so the MLE is 0.2 per second. With no events it is exp(−10λ), decreasing on λ > 0: the supremum is at the excluded boundary λ → 0, so no positive-rate MLE exists. Informative censoring requires a different observation model.

questions.title: The derivative missed the support
questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid uniform on \([0,\theta]\), \(\theta\) > 0, n ≥ 1. Use the density f(x;\(\theta\))=1/\(\theta\) for 0 ≤ x ≤ \(\theta\) and zero otherwise. Your observed maximum M is positive. A colleague differentiates −n log \(\theta\), finds no stationary point, and concludes that no MLE exists. Diagnose the error, derive the MLE, and decide whether it is unbiased.
hints: Could a proposed endpoint below an observed value have generated the record?
Optimize on the feasible support, then use the distribution of the sample maximum to check bias.
questions.solution: The full likelihood is \(\theta\)^(−n) times the indicator that \(\theta\) ≥ M. It is zero below M and decreases on [M,∞), so the MLE is M using the specified closed-support density. There is no need for an interior stationary point. Under the model P(M ≤ m)=\(\left(\frac m\theta\right)^n\) on \([0,\theta]\), so E[M]=\(\frac{n\theta}{n+1}\). M is downward biased; (n+1)M/n is unbiased but is not the likelihood maximizer. Likelihood fit and unbiasedness are different criteria.
questions.followup: What if the density convention instead excludes x=\(\theta\)? Does this change the probability law or the literal existence of a likelihood maximizer?
questions.followSolution: The probability law is unchanged because endpoints have probability zero. With the strict-support density \(\theta\) > M, the same supremum is approached as \(\theta\) decreases to M but is not attained. This subtlety is why the density version and parameter domain were specified. Regular asymptotic MLE arguments should not be applied automatically to a parameter-dependent support.

questions.title: One observation copied a hundred times
questions.prompt: One Bernoulli draw Y with unknown success probability p is observed to be 1. A pipeline copies it into 100 identical rows and fits an iid Bernoulli model. Compare the correct and naive likelihoods. Do their MLEs differ on [0,1]? Does agreement of the MLE mean the inferred precision is valid?
hints: There was one random draw. The copies are deterministic given it.
Compare likelihood ratios at p=0.5 and \(p=1\), not only the location of the maximum.
questions.solution: The correct likelihood is p, because the whole copied record occurs exactly when Y=1. The naive iid likelihood is p^100. Both maximize at \(p=1\) on [0,1], but the likelihood ratio of 0.5 to 1 is 0.5 in the real model and 2^(−100) in the naive one. Copying created apparent concentration without information. The endpoint also means an interior normal approximation is unjustified. Identical fitted estimates can hide a radically wrong uncertainty model.
questions.followup: In market data, distinct rows may still be dependent. How would you improve the model without claiming that every repeated value is a duplicate?
questions.followSolution: Identify the observation unit and sampling mechanism first. Distinguish true duplicate records from distinct events with identical values. A joint model may factor into conditional probabilities given history rather than marginal iid probabilities. Fit and validate an appropriate dependence model; use resampling or robust uncertainty methods only with assumptions matching that dependence. Row count alone is not effective sample size.

lessons.title: Count the right sample space
lessons.intro: Before calculating a probability, describe the experiment, what counts as one outcome, and why the outcomes have the probabilities you assign to them.

sections.title: Start with the experiment, outcomes and event
sections.text:
An experiment is the random procedure you carry out: for example, rolling one die or drawing two balls from a bag. An outcome records one possible result of that procedure. You must decide exactly what information the record contains.

The sample space, written \(\Omega\) and read “omega”, is the set of all possible outcomes. An event, written \(A\), is a collection of outcomes that satisfy a condition you care about.

For one fair six-sided die, \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). If the event is “roll an even number”, then \(A=\{2,4,6\}\). The notation \(|\Omega|\) means the number of outcomes in the sample space; \(|A|\) means the number of outcomes in the event. Here these counts are 6 and 3. The vertical bars mean “number of elements”, not absolute value, when their contents are a set.

sections.title: When counting gives a probability
sections.text:
If a finite sample space has equally likely outcomes, every outcome has probability \(1/|\Omega|\). Therefore,

\[P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.\]

Read this as “the probability of the event equals the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes”. For the even-number event above, \(P(A)=3/6=1/2\).

“Uniformly chosen” means that each outcome in the specified set has the same probability. It is an assumption about the sampling procedure, not a consequence of merely listing outcomes. A biased coin still has two possible outcomes, heads and tails, but counting one favourable outcome out of two does not establish a probability of one half. When outcomes are not equally likely, add their actual probabilities instead.

sections.title: Two dice: why the outcomes are ordered
sections.text:
Roll two independent fair six-sided dice, one red and one blue. Record an outcome as (red die value, blue die value). The outcome (2,5) differs from (5,2), because the values are assigned to different dice.

There are 6 choices for the red die and, for each choice, 6 choices for the blue die. Thus there are \(6\times6=36\) ordered outcomes. Fairness and independence make each ordered outcome have probability \((1/6)(1/6)=1/36\).

If you instead record only the sum, the possible sums are 2 through 12, but those eleven outcomes are not equally likely. Sum 2 comes only from (1,1), while sum 7 comes from six ordered outcomes. So \(P(\text{sum}=2)=1/36\) and \(P(\text{sum}=7)=6/36\), not one eleventh each. Your choice of sample space must preserve the probabilities.

sections.title: Drawing two balls: define n before counting
sections.text:
Suppose a bag contains \(n\) individually distinguishable balls, where \(n\geq2\). Draw one ball uniformly, keep it out of the bag, then draw a second ball uniformly from the remaining balls. This is sampling without replacement: the same physical ball cannot appear twice.

Now ignore the order in which the two balls were drawn. An unordered pair records which two balls you obtained; drawing A then B and drawing B then A produce the same pair, AB.

There are \(n\) choices for the first ball and \(n-1\) choices for the second, giving \(n(n-1)\) ordered selections. Every unordered pair is counted exactly twice in that total, once in each order. Divide by two:

\[\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.\]

The notation \(\binom{n}{2}\), read “n choose two”, counts the ways to select two different objects from n objects while ignoring order. For four balls labelled A, B, C and D, the six unordered pairs are AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD. The formula gives \(\binom{4}{2}=4\times3/2=6\).

Under the sampling procedure stated above, every unordered pair has the same probability: its two ordered selections each have probability \(1/[n(n-1)]\). Balls of the same colour are still different physical balls. Recording only the colours would group together different numbers of these equally likely pairs.

sections.title: Replacement changes the experiment
sections.text:
With replacement, you return the first ball before the second draw. Without replacement, you leave it out. These are different experiments and can give different probabilities for the same verbal event.

Suppose the bag contains 6 red balls and 4 blue balls, and the event is “the two colours differ”. Without replacement, a red-first draw leaves 4 blue balls among 9 remaining balls. A blue-first draw leaves 6 red balls among 9 remaining balls. The two possible colour orders cannot both occur, so add their probabilities:

\[P(\text{different colours})=\frac6{10}\frac49+\frac4{10}\frac69=\frac8{15}.\]

With replacement, the second draw again uses the original bag of 10 balls:

\[P(\text{different colours})=\frac6{10}\frac4{10}+\frac4{10}\frac6{10}=\frac{12}{25}.\]

The second denominator is 9 in the first experiment and 10 in the second. State the replacement rule before choosing a counting formula.

sections.title: Complements and overlapping events
sections.text:
The complement of an event A, written \(A^c\), contains all outcomes in which A does not happen. Since exactly one of A and its complement happens, \(P(A)=1-P(A^c)\).

For two independent fair coin flips, the equally likely ordered outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT, where H means heads and T means tails. “At least one head” includes HH, HT and TH. Its complement is “no heads”, which contains only TT. The probability is therefore \(1-1/4=3/4\). Listing the favourable outcomes gives the same result, \(3/4\).

For two events A and B, \(A\cup B\) means “A or B, including both”, and \(A\cap B\) means “both A and B”. The addition rule is

\[P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).\]

Adding the first two probabilities counts the overlap twice; subtracting it once corrects this. With the two dice above, let A mean “the red die is six” and B mean “the blue die is six”. Each event has probability \(1/6\); both happen with probability \(1/36\). Thus the chance of at least one six is \(1/6+1/6-1/36=11/36\).

sections.title: Independence and disjointness are different
sections.text:
Events are independent when learning that one happened does not change the probability of the other. Their joint probability then satisfies \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). Fairness describes one die's probabilities; independence describes how the dice relate to one another. Neither assumption replaces the other.

Events are disjoint when they cannot happen together, so \(P(A\cap B)=0\). For disjoint events, the addition rule reduces to \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)\).

For one die, “roll 1” and “roll 2” are disjoint. They are not independent: learning that the die rolled 1 makes the probability of rolling 2 zero. For two independent dice, “red die is six” and “blue die is six” are independent, but they are not disjoint because (6,6) satisfies both.

Before solving an interview problem, write down the experiment, the outcome you record, whether order matters, whether replacement is allowed, and the justification for equal likelihood or independence. Then identify the event and count or add probabilities.

lessons.example:
Work through the 6-red, 4-blue example using unordered pairs. There are 10 individually distinguishable balls in total, so \(n=10\). Draw two uniformly without replacement and ignore their order.

The total number of equally likely pairs is \(\binom{10}{2}=10\times9/2=45\). To obtain different colours, choose one of the 6 red balls and one of the 4 blue balls. This produces \(6\times4=24\) favourable unordered pairs; each red-blue pair is counted once. Therefore,

\[P(\text{different colours})=\frac{24}{45}=\frac8{15}.\]

This agrees with the red-then-blue plus blue-then-red calculation above. Both methods describe the same experiment. Counting only “red-red, red-blue, blue-blue” and assigning each probability one third would be wrong: those three colour categories contain different numbers of physical pairs.
lessons.check: For two independent fair coins, what is \(P(\text{at least one H})\)?
lessons.explanation: The four equally likely ordered outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Only TT has no heads. The probability of at least one head is 1 minus \(\frac{1}{4}\), which is \(\frac{3}{4}\).
objectives: Define an experiment, sample space and event before calculating.
Distinguish ordered and unordered sampling with and without replacement.
Justify equal likelihood and separate independence from disjointness.

lessons.title: Condition, then normalise
lessons.intro: Conditioning changes the information you are allowed to use. Rebuild the relevant population before calculating, then use Bayes to compare explanations of what you observed.

sections.title: What does “given” mean?
sections.text:
Let A and B be events in an experiment. The statement “given B” means that you know B happened, so outcomes outside B are no longer possible. You are computing a probability in that restricted population, not in the original one.

Provided \(P(B)>0\), define
\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.\]
The numerator is the probability mass that satisfies both conditions. Dividing by the mass of B rescales the restricted population so its total probability becomes one. If the original outcomes are equally likely, you may count favourable outcomes inside B. Otherwise, retain their probability weights.

The direction matters: “has a positive test given disease” and “has disease given a positive test” condition on different populations. They can have very different answers.

sections.title: A concrete conditional sample space
sections.text:
Roll two independent fair six-sided dice, with the first die distinguishable from the second. Before observing anything there are 36 equally likely ordered pairs. Now learn that the sum is 8. The surviving pairs are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2).

Each surviving pair originally had probability \(\frac{1}{36}\). Their total mass is \(\frac{5}{36}\), so each now has conditional probability one fifth. The event “the dice agree” contains only (4,4), giving \(P(\text{double}\mid\text{sum}=8)=1/5\).

Do not keep a denominator of 36: that would compute the chance of a double AND a sum of 8, before receiving the observation. The new question asks about an experiment whose outcome is already known to satisfy the sum constraint.

sections.title: Multiplication and total probability
sections.text:
Rearranging the definition gives \(P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)\). This identity does not require independence. Independence is the additional statement that conditioning on B does not change the probability of A.

Suppose hypotheses \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\) are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. For an observation D, split its probability into branches:
\[P(D)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}P(D\mid H_i)P(H_i).\]
You multiply along each branch and add across alternatives that cannot occur together. Check that the hypothesis list really covers the population. Omitting an alternative produces the wrong normalising denominator even if every multiplication is correct.

sections.title: Bayes: update weights, then normalise
sections.text:
The prior \(P(H_i)\) is a hypothesis's probability before D. The likelihood \(P(D\mid H_i)\) is the probability of the observation under that hypothesis. The posterior is its updated probability after D:
\[P(H_i\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid H_i)P(H_i)}{\sum_jP(D\mid H_j)P(H_j)}.\]
A reliable interview method is to write one unnormalised weight for each hypothesis, then divide each weight by their sum. A large likelihood alone does not establish a large posterior: a very rare hypothesis can still have little total weight.

For a fair coin and an always-heads coin selected with equal probability, observing one head gives weights (one half times one half) and (one half times one). Their sum is three quarters, so the always-heads posterior is two thirds.

sections.title: More observations require a sampling model
sections.text:
Keep the SAME selected coin for k flips. Conditional on the fair-coin hypothesis, assume flips are independent. Its likelihood for k consecutive heads is \(2^{-k}\); the always-heads likelihood is one. Equal priors therefore give
\[P(\text{always-heads}\mid k\text{ heads})=\frac{1}{1+2^{-k}}.\]
For k=2 the posterior is four fifths. This formula would not describe a procedure that selects a fresh coin before every flip. An observed tail assigns zero posterior weight to the always-heads hypothesis under this idealised model. If the “always-heads” coin actually has a small tail probability, zero is no longer justified.

Before multiplying likelihoods, ask what remains fixed and which observations are conditionally independent.

sections.title: Exact continuous observations need a different definition
sections.text:
The event formula divides by P(B), so it does not directly define conditioning on an exact value of a continuous variable when that event has probability zero. A continuous signal requires a conditional-density model or another appropriate conditional-probability construction.

For discrete hypotheses and a continuous signal s, posterior weights can use the signal DENSITY under each hypothesis: prior weight times density at s, then normalise. A density is not the probability of that exact signal; it describes probability per unit signal near s. Its value can exceed one without violating probability bounds.

This distinction prevents an otherwise sensible Bayes argument from dividing by zero or treating a density as an event probability. Match likelihoods to whether the observation is a discrete event, an interval or a continuous measurement.

sections.title: Conditioning can create dependence
sections.text:
The two dice were independent before you learned their sum. Given sum 8, if you learn that the first die is 2, the second must be 6. The observation couples variables that previously varied freely.

Conversely, observations can be independent conditional on a hidden hypothesis while being dependent before that hypothesis is known. Repeated heads suggest that the same hidden coin is favourable, changing the prediction of the next flip. Be explicit about whether an independence claim is unconditional or conditional on a specified variable.

Rehearse the argument aloud: state the observation, identify surviving possibilities or hypothesis weights, normalise, and check that the result lies between zero and one. Finally say which sampling assumption would change the answer.

lessons.example: Compare the two dice and coin examples. For dice, the observation removes ordered pairs; for coins, both hypotheses survive but with different weights. In the coin experiment, the joint mass of “always-heads and a head” is one half; the total head probability is three quarters. Dividing yields two thirds. Predict the next flip without picking the most likely coin as if it were certain: \(P(\text{next H}\mid\text{first H})=(2/3)\times1+(1/3)\times(1/2)=5/6\). The posterior still retains uncertainty about the coin.
lessons.check: After seeing H from this mixture, what is \(P(\text{always-heads})\)?
lessons.explanation: The always-heads branch contributes probability \(\frac{1}{2}\); the fair branch contributes \(\frac{1}{4}\). Normalise the first weight by their sum \(\frac{3}{4}\) to obtain \(\frac{2}{3}\).
objectives: Build a conditional sample space and normalise its probabilities.
Distinguish likelihood, prior and posterior.
Explain why conditioning can create dependence.

lessons.title: Expectation without independence
lessons.intro: Expectation is a probability-weighted average. Its linearity lets you break complicated counts into simple indicators, even when their events overlap.

sections.title: A random variable and its mean
sections.text:
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome. For a discrete variable X with possible values x, its expectation is \(E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x)\), whenever the expectation is well defined. A fair die has expectation (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5. The mean need not itself be a possible realised value.

For ordinary signed variables, absolute integrability, \(E[|X|]<\infty\), is a convenient condition that makes sums and rearrangements safe. Nonnegative variables can have an infinite expectation; the formula then describes an extended value rather than a finite average. State the assumption before manipulating an infinite series.

sections.title: Why linearity works
sections.text:
For integrable variables X and Y and constants a and b,
\[E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y].\]
This follows by averaging the linear expression outcome by outcome. It does not require X and Y to be independent. If Y always equals X, the variables are maximally dependent, yet the mean of their sum is still twice the mean of X.

Independence is needed for other shortcuts. In general \(E[XY]\) does not equal \(E[X]E[Y]\). For a fair die X, the expectation of its square is \(\frac{91}{6}\), whereas the square of its expectation is 12.25. Always distinguish a sum, a product and a nonlinear transformation before selecting a rule.

sections.title: Indicators convert events into arithmetic
sections.text:
For an event A, its indicator \(I_A\) is one when A happens and zero otherwise. Hence \(E[I_A]=P(A)\). If a count C records how many of m events occur, write \(C=\sum_{i=1}^{m}I_i\). Linearity then gives
\[E[C]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}P(I_i=1).\]
You only need each event's individual probability to compute this mean. The indicators may overlap or share a common cause. A useful first step in a counting problem is to ask what one indicator should count: a position, an object, a pair or a distinct category. Choosing the wrong unit can double-count or omit events.

sections.title: Overlapping heads, carefully counted
sections.text:
Flip a fair coin independently 20 times. Let \(I_i\) indicate that flips i and i+1 are both heads, for i from 1 through 19. There are 19 possible adjacent positions, not 20. Each position is HH with probability one quarter, so the expected number of adjacent HH pairs is \(\frac{19}{4}=4.75\).

The sequence HHH contributes two pairs, at its first and second positions. Adjacent indicators are dependent because they share a flip, but their expectations still add. If the head probability is p with independent flips, the corresponding expectation is \((n-1)p^2\) for n flips. If flips are dependent, linearity still works but the individual pair probability may cease to be p squared.

sections.title: Tail sums: count how many thresholds are crossed
sections.text:
For a nonnegative integer-valued variable N, a realised value of three can be written as three ones: it exceeds or equals thresholds 1, 2 and 3. Thus \(N=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}I_{\{N\geq k\}}\), giving
\[E[N]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(N\geq k).\]
Nonnegativity justifies this interchange even if the result is infinite. For a nonnegative continuous variable X, the analogous identity is
\[E[X]=\int_0^{\infty}P(X>t)\,dt.\]
The area under the survival curve represents the mean. Do not apply these nonnegative formulas unchanged to a variable that can take negative values. Separate its positive and negative parts and check finiteness.

sections.title: The maximum of two dice
sections.text:
Let M be the larger of two independent fair dice. For integer k from 1 through 6, both dice are at most k with probability \(P(M\leq k)=k^2/36\). Subtract successive cumulative probabilities to obtain
\[P(M=k)=\frac{k^2-(k-1)^2}{36}=\frac{2k-1}{36}.\]
Multiplying each k by this probability and summing yields \(\frac{161}{36}\), approximately 4.4722. A maximum preferentially selects larger outcomes, so the maximum of the means, 3.5, is not the expected maximum.

As a check, the minimum plus maximum equals the sum of the two dice in every outcome. Their expectations must therefore sum to seven, giving an expected minimum of \(\frac{91}{36}\). This uses a pointwise identity, not an independence assumption about minimum and maximum.

sections.title: What linearity does not tell you
sections.text:
A mean does not describe fluctuation around that mean. For a sum, variance contains covariance terms. With n independent fair flips, the HH-count variance is \((5n-7)/16\) for n at least two: each indicator contributes variance \(\frac{3}{16}\) and each adjacent pair contributes covariance \(\frac{1}{16}\) twice in the sum formula.

You will derive that variance machinery in the dependence lesson. For now, identify exactly where dependence mattered: not in adding means, but in relating indicators jointly. Practise explaining both the short solution and why the longer independence argument is unnecessary.

lessons.example: For two dice, compute the maximum's weighted sum explicitly: the numerator is \(1\times1+2\times3+3\times5+4\times7+5\times9+6\times11=161\), and the denominator is 36. A second route uses \(P(M\geq k)=1-(k-1)^2/36\) for k=1 through 6. Summing gives \(6-(0+1+4+9+16+25)/36=161/36\). Matching two methods is a useful interview check; neither treats the maximum as a fair die.
lessons.check: Do overlapping indicators prevent adding their expectations?
options: Only if they have equal means
lessons.explanation: Linearity of expectation does not require independence.
objectives: Define expectation and turn a count into indicators.
Use linearity without inventing independence.
Derive discrete and continuous tail-sum identities.
