lessons.title: Distributions as usable models
lessons.intro: A distribution is a model for how an experiment produces outcomes. Learn its assumptions, support and probabilities before memorising its mean.

sections.title: Describe the distribution before using a formula
sections.text:
For a random variable X, the cumulative distribution function is \(F_X(x)=P(X\leq x)\). Its survival probability is \(P(X>x)=1-F_X(x)\). A discrete probability mass function assigns probabilities to individual values. A continuous density assigns probability through integration over intervals; a density value itself is not a point probability.

Specify the support: the set of allowed values. A \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) variable takes values between zero and one, with constant density one there. Its CDF is zero below zero, x on the unit interval and one above one. An exponential waiting time is nonnegative and unbounded. Mixing these supports is a common source of incorrect integrals.

sections.title: Independent uniform draws and the maximum
sections.text:
Draw n independent \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) variables \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\), with n a positive integer. Let M be their maximum. For x between zero and one, M is at most x precisely when every draw is at most x. Independence gives
\[P(M\leq x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(U_i\leq x)=x^n.\]
Its density is \(nx^{n-1}\) on this interval, obtained by differentiating the CDF. The tail-integral identity also gives
\[E[M]=\int_0^1(1-x^n)\,dx=\frac{n}{n+1}.\]
For one draw the mean is one half; increasing n moves the expected maximum toward one. Both checks are consistent with the experiment.

sections.title: The minimum uses survival probabilities
sections.text:
Let m be the minimum of the same independent draws. The event m>x requires every draw to exceed x, so \(P(m>x)=(1-x)^n\) for x in the unit interval. Therefore,
\[E[m]=\int_0^1(1-x)^n\,dx=\frac{1}{n+1}.\]
For three draws, the minimum's mean is one quarter and the maximum's is three quarters. Those symmetric means result from the \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) model. They are not a general minimum/maximum rule for arbitrary distributions.

If all n draws are actually copies of one shared uniform variable, the independence multiplication fails. The minimum and maximum then both equal that variable and both have mean one half, regardless of n.

sections.title: Exponential waiting times and units
sections.text:
A waiting time T has exponential rate \(\lambda>0\) when its survival probability is \(P(T>t)=e^{-\lambda t}\) for t at least zero. Its density is \(\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\), and integrating the survival curve gives \(E[T]=1/\lambda\).

Rate and mean are different parameters. A rate of two arrivals per minute produces a mean wait of half a minute. A rate of one half per minute produces a mean wait of two minutes. The exponent must be dimensionless: rate times time has no units.

A constant exponential rate models a wait whose instantaneous chance of ending does not depend on its age. Real waits need not satisfy this assumption.

sections.title: Memorylessness: remaining time is not total time
sections.text:
For nonnegative s and t,
\[P(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}}=e^{-\lambda t}.\]
Conditional on already waiting s, the remaining wait has the same exponential distribution as a fresh wait. Consequently its expected remaining time is \(\frac1{\text{rate}}\), while expected total time is s plus \(\frac1{\text{rate}}\).

With rate one half per minute and three minutes already elapsed, remaining expectation is two and total expectation is five. This distinction is the whole point of that interview question. For a wait uniformly distributed between zero and ten minutes, surviving past minute nine instead leaves a mean of half a minute; memorylessness fails.

sections.title: Competing independent clocks
sections.text:
Let X and Y be independent exponential waits with rates a and b, respectively. Their minimum exceeds t when both exceed t, so its survival is \(e^{-at}e^{-bt}=e^{-(a+b)t}\). The first ring therefore has exponential rate a+b.

The chance that X wins is
\[P(X<Y)=\int_0^\infty ae^{-at}e^{-bt}\,dt=\frac{a}{a+b}.\]
The integrand combines “X rings around t” with “Y has not rung yet”. Ties have probability zero for these continuous waits. This ratio assumes independent clocks and constant exponential rates; it is not a universal race formula for any waiting-time distributions.

sections.title: Geometric probability depends on the experiment
sections.text:
For the stick-cutting problem, choose two independent uniform positions on a unit stick, then order them as \(U<V\). The three lengths are U, V-U and 1-V. A nondegenerate triangle requires every piece to be less than one half.

The ordered cut locations occupy a triangle of area one half. The valid region satisfies \(U<\frac12\), \(V>\frac12\) and V-\(U<\frac12\), with area one eighth. Their ratio is one quarter. Boundary equalities have probability zero.

Choosing an existing piece first and then cutting that piece defines another experiment and another distribution. Always derive the density on the region you are measuring instead of assuming that every visually plausible region is uniform.

lessons.example: Take two independent exponential clocks with rates three and two per minute. Their first ring has rate five per minute and expected time one fifth of a minute. The rate-three clock wins with probability three fifths. These are different objects: a time and a probability. Their joint density for “clock one wins at time t” is \(3e^{-5t}\), which factors into \((3/5)(5e^{-5t})\). Under this specific model the winner and first-ring time are independent.
lessons.check: Given an Exponential(rate 2) wait has exceeded 5, what is the expected remaining wait?
lessons.explanation: Memorylessness gives a fresh expected wait of \(\frac{1}{2}\).
objectives: Distinguish probability mass, density, CDF and survival.
Derive the extremes of independent uniform draws.
Explain exponential memorylessness and competing clocks.

lessons.title: A state is a sufficient memory
lessons.intro: Overlapping patterns and stopping problems become manageable when you retain exactly the history that affects the future. Turn that history into states and write first-step equations.

sections.title: What are you counting, and when do you stop?
sections.text:
A stopping time is a random time whose decision to stop can be made from observations available so far. Counting flips until the first HH pattern is a stopping-time problem. Deciding at time five whether to stop because flip six will be heads uses future information and is not a stopping time with respect to the observed flips.

State the convention: our wait includes every flip, including the final flips completing the pattern. Distinguish an expected stopping time from a probability of eventually stopping. A process can stop with probability one yet have infinite expected duration. Do not assume a finite answer merely because a recurrence can be written.

sections.title: Choose a sufficient state
sections.text:
Flip a fair coin independently until HH occurs. Before finishing, there are two useful states: state 0 means no trailing head, and state H means the latest flip was a head. State HH is terminal. Earlier history does not change future transition probabilities because the coin flips are independent and only the suffix matters for matching HH.

Let E0 and EH be expected additional flips from the two nonterminal states. The terminal state's expected additional wait is zero. Be precise about “additional”: EH is not the total number of flips already spent reaching H. This choice prevents adding elapsed time twice.

sections.title: First-step equations and their solution
sections.text:
From state 0, pay one flip. A tail leaves you in 0 and a head moves you to H, each with probability one half. From H, a head finishes while a tail returns to 0. Hence
\[E_0=1+\frac{E_0+E_H}{2},\qquad E_H=1+\frac{E_0}{2}.\]
The first equation gives \(E_0=2+E_H\). Substitute the second: \(E_0=3+E_0/2\), so E0=6 and EH=4.

The tempting answer four is the reciprocal of the probability of HH in a fixed two-flip window. Consecutive windows overlap and are not fresh independent attempts. A tail can destroy partial progress; the state recurrence records that information.

sections.title: Why HT has a different waiting time
sections.text:
For HT, retain state H again. From H, a tail finishes and another head leaves the useful suffix H. Thus \(E_H=1+E_H/2\), giving EH=2. The state-0 equation is unchanged, so E0=4.

For HHH, use states with zero, one and two trailing heads. Every tail returns to zero. With terminal wait zero, the equations are
\[E_0=1+(E_0+E_1)/2,\quad E_1=1+(E_0+E_2)/2,\quad E_2=1+E_0/2.\]
Solving yields E0=14. The probability of a particular HHH window is one eighth, but the expected wait is not eight. The distinction between a fixed-window event and a sequential search must remain visible in your explanation.

sections.title: Prove that the wait has a finite mean
sections.text:
For HH, split flips into nonoverlapping blocks of two. Each block is HH with probability one quarter, independently across blocks. Waiting for the first successful block has geometric mean four blocks, or eight flips. The actual HH search stops no later than that block procedure, so its expectation is at most eight and is finite.

This bound is not the exact answer six. Its job is to justify treating the expected-state equations as finite quantities. Similar block arguments work for any fixed finite pattern with positive probability under independent flips. For processes with unbounded states, finiteness may require a different argument.

sections.title: Collecting symbols by stages
sections.text:
Suppose each independent draw returns one of m equally likely symbols, with m a positive integer. After seeing k distinct symbols, a new symbol arrives with probability (m-k)/m. The stage wait is geometric, counting the successful draw, and has mean m/(m-k).

Add expected stage durations using linearity:
\[E[T]=m\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac1j.\]
For four symbols the terms are 1, \(\frac{4}{3}\), 2 and 4, summing to \(\frac{25}{3}\). Unequal symbol probabilities change the success rate according to WHICH symbols you have seen, not only their count. The state “k distinct symbols” then ceases to be sufficient.

sections.title: A bounded random walk
sections.text:
A fair integer random walk moves one step left or right with equal probability and stops at 0 or N, where N is a positive integer. Let ti be the expected additional steps from position i. The boundary conditions are t0=tN=0 and
\[t_i=1+\frac{t_{i-1}+t_{i+1}}2.\]
The quadratic \(t_i=i(N-i)\) satisfies both the recurrence and boundaries. For N=12 and i=5 it gives 35. A finite interval and positive chance of reaching a boundary in a bounded number of steps imply a finite expected exit time.

For the probability of hitting N first, omit the one-step cost and use boundary probabilities zero and one. The solution is i/N. Means and hitting probabilities solve different equations; identify your target before writing the recurrence.

lessons.example: Solve HH again using a different counting convention. If you have just seen a head, a second head ends the search next flip; a tail consumes one flip and puts you back at the start. Thus EH=1+E0/2. At the start, E0=1+(E0+EH)/2. Solve to obtain EH=4 and E0=6. Explain out loud why EH is still four additional flips even though one head has already been observed: a tail may erase that progress and restart a six-flip expected search.
lessons.check: What is the expected wait for HH in fair coin flips?
lessons.explanation: A tail erases a partial match; solving the two state equations gives 6.
objectives: Define states, terminal conditions and first-step recurrences.
Solve overlapping-pattern waits without treating windows as independent trials.
Check finite expectation and solve a bounded random walk.

lessons.title: Arithmetic with a method
lessons.intro: Mental arithmetic improves when you choose a structure before calculating. Build accuracy with decompositions, reciprocal anchors and checks, then train speed on the same methods.

sections.title: Accuracy first: represent the calculation
sections.text:
Mental math is not only recalling multiplication tables. It is choosing an equivalent expression that uses easier numbers and remembering the intermediate values reliably. Start a drill with a method you can explain; a fast wrong answer is not progress.

For 49 times 21, replace 49 by 50 minus one. Compute 50 times 21 as 1050, then subtract 21 to obtain 1029. The subtraction corrects the deliberate overestimate. If you subtract 49 instead, you are correcting the wrong factor. State what you changed before calculating its correction.

sections.title: Distribute, then compensate
sections.text:
The distributive identity \((a+b)c=ac+bc\) is the basic tool. For 23 times 14, use 23 times (10+4), giving 230+92=322. For 99 times 37, use 100 times 37 minus 37, giving 3663.

When both factors lie near the same anchor, the difference-of-squares identity can be shorter:
\[(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2.\]
Thus 97 times 103 equals 100 squared minus 3 squared, or 9991. The factors must be equally far below and above the anchor. For 97 times 104, that identity does not apply directly; use 100 times 104 minus 3 times 104, giving 10088.

sections.title: Percentages are fractions of the base
sections.text:
A percentage p means p/100 of the stated base. Fifteen percent of 240 is ten percent plus five percent: 24+12=36. Eighteen percent of 250 is ten percent plus eight percent: 25+20=45. You may also exchange the operands: 18% of 250 equals 250% of 18, because both are the same product divided by 100.

Always identify the base. Increasing 100 by 20% gives 120. Decreasing that new value by 20% gives 96, not 100, because the second percentage applies to a different base. A relative change uses the original value in the denominator; a difference between percentages may instead be measured in percentage points.

sections.title: Fractions: exact values and decimal anchors
sections.text:
Keep common exact anchors available: one half is 0.5, one quarter 0.25, one fifth 0.2 and one eighth 0.125. Three eighths is three times 0.125=0.375. One sixteenth is half of one eighth=0.0625.

One sixth has repeating decimal 0.1666…, so 0.1667 is an approximation, not an equality. One seventh repeats the block 142857. Use a fraction when exactness matters; give a rounded decimal only with a stated precision.

For fractions with the same denominator, combine numerators before converting. Five twelfths plus seven twelfths equals one exactly. Converting each to a short rounded decimal can introduce an unnecessary rounding error.

sections.title: Division and cancellation
sections.text:
Division is multiplication by a reciprocal, but cancelling common factors is often easier. For 84 divided by 12, both numbers divide by three, reducing the problem to 28 divided by four, or seven. For 2.4 divided by 0.06, multiply numerator and denominator by 100 to obtain 240 divided by six, or forty.

Changing only the denominator changes the problem. When decimal places differ, write the common scaling operation explicitly. For \(\frac{15}{24}\), cancel a factor of three to obtain \(\frac{5}{8}\)=0.625.

Approximate before doing a difficult division. Since 19 is slightly less than 20, 380 divided by 19 must be slightly more than 19; the exact value is twenty. A result near two or two hundred would fail the magnitude check.

sections.title: Check the answer without repeating the same mistake
sections.text:
Use an independent check: magnitude, last digit, reverse multiplication or a nearby anchor. For 49 times 21, the result should lie just below 50 times 21=1050 and end in nine. The answer 1029 meets both tests. For a probability, the result must lie between zero and one; that check catches many arithmetic failures but cannot prove the model is correct.

Avoid rounding too early in a chain of operations. If a trainer accepts fractions, an exact fraction is often safer than a decimal truncated to too few places. In an interview, state when your answer is an approximation and give an error scale when that matters.

sections.title: Turn a short session into deliberate practice
sections.text:
Start with untimed accuracy, then use a short timed round at a manageable difficulty. Review errors by cause: wrong sign, lost intermediate value, poor decomposition or premature rounding. Repeat the METHOD, rather than memorising only that one question's answer.

Compare both accuracy and correct answers per minute across similar rounds. A higher attempt rate paired with sharply lower accuracy may indicate rushing. Stopped rounds have a different duration from completed rounds, so compare pace as well as counts.

Rotate mental arithmetic and fraction conversion. Explain one mistake in writing after each session. The aim is reliable number sense you can use while reasoning about a harder probability or statistical problem.

lessons.example: Work out 15% of 240 in three ways: 10%+5% gives 24+12=36; 0.15 times 240 gives 36; and 240% of 15 is 2.4 times 15=36. Now calculate 97 times 103 using the symmetric anchor: \((100-3)(100+3)=10000-9=9991\). Check that it lies below 10000 and ends in one. These checks support the arithmetic; they do not replace the derivation.
lessons.check: What is 15% of 240?
lessons.explanation: 10% is 24 and 5% is 12; add them.
objectives: Choose efficient decompositions for products and percentages.
Convert between fractions and decimals with stated precision.
Use magnitude checks and measured practice to improve speed.

lessons.title: Variance remembers dependence
lessons.intro: Averages reduce idiosyncratic noise, but shared variation can remain. Build variance from its definition and keep covariance terms when observations move together.

sections.title: Variance measures squared deviations
sections.text:
For a variable X with finite second moment and mean mu, variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]\). Expanding the square gives \(E[X^2]-E[X]^2\). Its units are the square of X's units; standard deviation is the square root and has the original units.

If you shift every value by a constant b, deviations from the shifted mean are unchanged. Scaling by a multiplies deviations by a, so
\[\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).\]
With variance four, multiplying by three and adding two produces variance 36, not fourteen. The additive constant changes the mean, not dispersion.

sections.title: Covariance records joint movement
sections.text:
For variables X and Y with finite second moments, covariance is \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])]\). Positive covariance means positive and negative deviations tend to align; negative covariance means they tend to oppose each other. Covariance has the product of the variables' units.

When both variances are positive, correlation is covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations. It is unitless and lies between minus one and one. If either variable is constant, that denominator vanishes and ordinary correlation is undefined.

Independence implies zero covariance when moments exist. Zero covariance alone does not imply independence: a symmetric variable and its square can have zero covariance while being deterministically related.

sections.title: Expand a sum before applying shortcuts
sections.text:
Subtract the means, square the sum and take expectations:
\[\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).\]
For a weighted sum of m variables, the general form is
\[\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_i a_iX_i\right)=\sum_i\sum_j a_i a_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).\]
The diagonal terms are individual variances. Each distinct unordered pair contributes twice, once as (i,j) and once as (j,i). Do not combine an ordered double sum with another extra factor of two.

If X and Y each have variance one and correlation one, they fluctuate together and the sum has variance four. The independence shortcut would give two.

sections.title: Variance of the arithmetic mean
sections.text:
For n observations, define \(\bar X=(X_1+\cdots+X_n)/n\). Applying the scaling and sum rules gives
\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).\]
Under independence and a common variance sigma squared, only n diagonal terms remain, giving variance sigma squared divided by n. Without independence, count the off-diagonal terms too.

This is a statement about repeated samples of the estimator. It is not the sample variance of the observed numbers themselves. The standard error of the mean estimates the square root of this sampling variance.

sections.title: Equicorrelation and the common component
sections.text:
Assume every observation has variance \(\sigma^2>0\), and every distinct pair has the same correlation rho. There are n diagonal terms and n(n-1) ordered off-diagonal terms. Thus
\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2\left[\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{n}\right].\]
For \(n=100\), variance one and rho=0.1, the result is 0.109, not 0.01. As n grows, variance approaches 0.1. Averaging cannot eliminate a component shared by every observation.

For nonnegative rho, a concrete representation is \(X_i=Z+\epsilon_i\), with independent common shock Z and idiosyncratic noises, variances rho times sigma squared and (1-rho) times sigma squared. Averaging reduces the noises, while Z remains.

sections.title: Not every correlation specification is possible
sections.text:
An equicorrelation matrix must be positive semidefinite. Its common-direction eigenvalue is \(1+(n-1)\rho\), and the other n-1 eigenvalues are 1-rho. Nonnegative eigenvalues require
\[-\frac{1}{n-1}\leq\rho\leq1\qquad(n>1).\]
For 100 variables, pairwise correlation minus one tenth is impossible even though it lies inside the ordinary two-variable range. It would make the proposed mean variance negative.

The lower bound produces a zero-variance sum in the singular boundary case. Correlations constrain one another collectively; the covariance-matrix lesson develops this point further.

sections.title: Apply the same reasoning to overlapping counts
sections.text:
In independent fair coin flips, each HH indicator has mean one quarter and variance three sixteenths. Adjacent indicators jointly occur when three consecutive flips are heads, with probability one eighth. Their covariance is one eighth minus one sixteenth, or one sixteenth. Indicators at disjoint positions are independent.

For n flips with n at least two, the count has n-1 indicator variances and n-2 adjacent covariance pairs. Its variance is \(3(n-1)/16+2(n-2)/16=(5n-7)/16\). This illustrates exactly why linearity simplified the mean but did not remove dependence from the variance.

lessons.example: Compare 100 independent variance-one observations with 100 equicorrelated observations at rho=0.1. Their mean variances are 0.01 and 0.109; their standard errors are 0.1 and approximately 0.3302. The standard-error ratio is \(\sqrt{10.9}\), approximately 3.30. Do not compare the variance ratio as if it were the standard-error ratio. Explain what common variation remains when the sample size becomes very large.
lessons.check: What is \(\operatorname{Var}(3X+2)\) when \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=4\)?
lessons.explanation: Multiply variance by \(3^2\); the shift adds no variance.
objectives: Define variance, covariance and correlation with their units.
Derive the variance of a dependent mean.
Explain the common-shock limit and feasible correlation bounds.

lessons.title: Write data code that respects time
lessons.intro: A correct-looking calculation can use information that was not yet available. Treat time, boundaries and reproducibility as part of the algorithm.

sections.title: Write an input and output contract
sections.text:
Before coding, define what each input represents, its ordering and the intended output at every index. Specify empty inputs, duplicate timestamps, missing values and ties. A short example often reveals an ambiguity that a long implementation would hide.

For a rolling mean, “window three” is incomplete. Does the result at index i include the value at i, or only the three previous observations? What happens before three previous values exist? Write those rules first. In an interview, a clarified contract is evidence of reasoning, not a delay before the real work.

sections.title: Three timestamps describe different facts
sections.text:
Event time is when something happened in the source system. Availability time is when the feature reached the system making a decision. Decision time is when that system chose an action. If a feature's event time is 10:00:00 but it arrives at 10:00:02, a decision at 10:00:01 cannot use it.

Sorting and joining only by event time may introduce future information even when every join operation is mechanically correct. Preserve both event and availability timestamps when they differ. For historical revised data, distinguish a first published value from a later revision; the final cleaned database may not describe what was knowable earlier.

sections.title: A causal rolling window
sections.text:
Let values be x0, x1 and so on, and let w be a positive integer window size. A lagged mean at index i uses exactly the previous w observations: indices i-w through i-1, excluding i. Define a missing result when i<w unless the task explicitly allows a shorter initial window.

For values [2,4,6,8] and w=3, the first complete lagged mean occurs at i=3 and equals four, from [2,4,6]. A window including the current eight instead gives six. Both are arithmetic means; only one matches the specified timing contract.

A running sum removes the oldest value and adds the newly eligible previous value. Confirm that subtraction and addition use the same boundary convention as the slow reference implementation.

sections.title: As-of joins use the available history
sections.text:
For each decision time, select the most recent feature whose availability time is no later than that decision. Decide whether an exactly equal timestamp is allowed and how same-time ties are resolved. “At or before” is appropriate only if the feature was accessible at that instant under the system's timestamp convention.

With sorted features and decisions, maintain a pointer into the feature stream. Advance it while the next feature is eligible, then emit the latest eligible value. Both pointers move only forward, so total work is linear in the number of records after sorting. Before the first available feature, return the task's explicit missing-value representation.

A fast join on the wrong timestamp is still wrong. Complexity and information validity answer different questions.

sections.title: Reference implementation before optimisation
sections.text:
Start with a small transparent function that scans the available history for every decision. It may be slow, but its logic should directly express the contract. Compare the optimised two-pointer algorithm against that function on hand-built cases.

Include a feature arriving between two decisions, an exact-time tie, a decision before any feature, two revisions of one event and repeated decision timestamps. For windows, include size one, an input shorter than the window and constant data. Use assertions about eligibility as well as expected numbers: every selected feature must have been available by its decision.

Do not manufacture expected outputs by calling the same implementation being tested; that only repeats its assumptions.

sections.title: Numerical and operational reproducibility
sections.text:
A calculation should identify its data version, transformation parameters and time conventions. If a simulation contributes a feature, record the seed and sampling method. If floating-point sums are used, distinguish exact mathematical identities from approximate numerical equality.

Keep a simple baseline and reconcile a handful of records manually. A complicated notebook can hide a one-row offset behind persuasive charts. A reproducible research function should make it possible to inspect what inputs produced one output without reconstructing the whole project.

Passing the provided examples proves behaviour on those cases. It does not establish that every boundary, every time convention or every asymptotic complexity claim is correct.

sections.title: Explain the solution as a sequence of invariants
sections.text:
For a two-pointer join, the invariant is that the selected feature is the latest eligible one among all records passed by the feature pointer. For a rolling window, it is that the running sum contains exactly the specified eligible indices. State why initialization establishes the invariant and why each update preserves it.

Then separate time for sorting from time for the scan: an unsorted input may require sorting even though the join itself is linear. State auxiliary memory independently of output storage. The interview explanation should connect the code to the information boundary and the complexity argument.

lessons.example: A feature has event time 10:00:00, availability time 10:00:02 and value seven. At decision 10:00:01, output no available value if there is no older eligible feature. At 10:00:02, use seven only if equality is explicitly allowed; at 10:00:03 it is eligible. A later revision arriving at 10:00:05 must not alter what the earlier decisions could have used. Build these four cases into a reference test before implementing the fast scan.

options: Its event time in all cases
Its availability time at the decision point
lessons.explanation: Availability defines the actual information set.
objectives: Separate event time, availability time and decision time.
Define causal rolling windows and as-of joins precisely.

lessons.title: Estimators, bias and uncertainty
lessons.intro: An estimator is a rule applied to a random sample. Assess its repeated-sample behaviour separately from the particular value your dataset produced.

sections.title: Parameter, estimator and estimate
sections.text:
A parameter describes a population or model: a mean mu, success probability p or endpoint theta. An estimator is a function of random observations, such as their arithmetic mean. An estimate is the numerical result after you observe one dataset. The parameter is fixed in a frequentist sampling calculation; the estimator varies across possible samples.

For n independent identically distributed observations with mean mu and variance sigma squared, the sample mean is unbiased because its expectation is mu. Its sampling variance is sigma squared divided by n. The actual estimate from one sample can still be far from mu. Unbiasedness is an average property across repeated samples, not a guarantee about one result.

sections.title: Bias and variance describe different errors
sections.text:
For estimator T of parameter theta, define \(\operatorname{Bias}(T)=E[T]-\theta\). Its variance describes fluctuation around its own mean. A perfectly constant wrong estimator has zero variance but nonzero bias.

Mean squared error measures squared distance from the target:
\[\operatorname{MSE}(T)=E[(T-\theta)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(T)+\operatorname{Bias}(T)^2.\]
To derive this, write T-theta as (T-E[T])+(E[T]-theta), expand the square and observe that the cross term has expectation zero. This identity requires the relevant second moment to be finite. Reducing bias can increase variance, so unbiasedness alone does not rank estimators by MSE.

sections.title: A maximum that underestimates an endpoint
sections.text:
Draw n independent Uniform(0,theta) observations, with theta positive and n a positive integer. Let M be their maximum. It cannot exceed theta, and typically falls below it. Scaling the uniform-maximum result gives
\[E[M]=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta.\]
The bias is minus theta/(n+1). Multiplying by \(\frac{n+1}{n}\) yields an unbiased endpoint estimator. This correction follows from the assumed independent uniform model; it does not automatically apply to an arbitrary bounded distribution.

Notice why a common intuition fails: being close to the largest observation does not make an endpoint estimate unbiased. The random unobserved gap between the maximum and the endpoint has a positive mean.

sections.title: Standard deviation versus standard error
sections.text:
The standard deviation of individual observations describes their population spread. The standard error of an estimator describes how its value varies across repeated datasets. For an iid sample mean with finite variance, estimate its standard error by the sample standard deviation divided by the square root of n.

For iid observations, the usual sample variance with denominator n-1 is unbiased for the population variance. The correction accounts for estimating the sample mean from the same observations. This does not mean its square root is an unbiased standard-deviation estimator.

If observations are dependent, the sample-mean standard error must include covariance terms. A large number of rows is not automatically a large amount of independent information.

sections.title: What a central limit theorem supplies
sections.text:
For iid observations with finite mean mu and positive finite variance sigma squared, the classical central limit theorem says
\[\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)}{\sigma}\Rightarrow N(0,1).\]
The arrow means convergence in distribution as n grows. It does not claim that observations themselves become Gaussian. It concerns a centred and scaled sample mean.

The normal approximation can be poor in a finite sample, especially with highly skewed or heavy-tailed observations. Infinite-variance data fall outside this classical theorem. Dependence requires different assumptions and often a different asymptotic variance. State both the object converging and the assumptions; “large sample” alone is not a theorem.

sections.title: Bayesian estimation uses an explicit prior
sections.text:
Now model Bernoulli trials with an unknown common success probability p. A Beta(alpha,beta) prior, with positive parameters alpha and beta, has density proportional to \(p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\) on the unit interval. Its mean is alpha divided by alpha+beta.

Observe s successes and f failures, conditionally independent given p. Multiplying prior density by the likelihood gives a Beta(alpha+s,beta+f) posterior. This exponent addition is the conjugate update, not a memorised adjustment with unexplained pseudo-counts.

With \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\), three successes and one failure produce \(\operatorname{Beta}(5,3)\), with mean \(\frac{5}{8}\). The sample proportion is \(\frac{3}{4}\). The posterior mean differs because it combines the prior with four observations. The next-trial predictive success probability is the posterior mean under this shared-p model.

sections.title: Interpret an uncertainty statement
sections.text:
A frequentist confidence interval is built by a sampling procedure with a stated long-run coverage rate under its assumptions. After observing a particular interval, the fixed parameter is either inside it or outside it. A Bayesian credible interval assigns posterior probability to parameter values conditional on the observed data and prior.

Both require a valid model; neither repairs selection bias or leakage. When explaining an estimate, give its target, sampling assumptions, method and uncertainty, then identify which source of uncertainty was omitted. Prediction uncertainty for a new observation also includes its own noise, so it is usually different from uncertainty about a population mean.

lessons.example: For a Bernoulli probability with \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\) prior and data containing three successes and one failure, write the unnormalised posterior as \(p^{1+3}(1-p)^{1+1}=p^4(1-p)^2\). Those exponents correspond to \(\operatorname{Beta}(5,3)\), not Beta(4,2). Its mean is \(\frac{5}{8}\)=0.625. Predict a new trial by averaging its conditional success probability p over the posterior, giving the same 0.625. State that the trials share one common p; a changing probability would need a different model.
lessons.check: Which criterion combines variance and squared bias?
lessons.explanation: \[\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta)=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)+\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2.\]
objectives: Distinguish parameters, estimators, estimates and uncertainty.
Derive the bias–variance decomposition of mean squared error.
Work through a biased maximum estimator and a Beta posterior update.

lessons.title: Let the data compare the models
lessons.intro: Hold the observations fixed, vary the model, and derive what maximum likelihood really estimates. Then challenge the assumptions behind the answer.

sections.title: One record, several explanations
sections.text: For ten independent Bernoulli trials with a common success probability p, observe seven successes. The likelihood of the specified ordered record is p^7(1-p)^3. Compare candidate values of p while holding that record fixed.

sections.title: A likelihood is not a posterior
sections.text: A probability model varies possible data at a fixed parameter. A likelihood varies the parameter at fixed observed data. A continuous likelihood uses a density, not the probability of an exact point. Relative likelihood is a ratio to the best-fitting value, not a parameter probability.

sections.title: Derive the optimum
sections.text: For n trials and k successes, the log-likelihood is \(\ell(p)=k\log p+(n-k)\log(1-p)\). The interior optimum is \(\hat p=k/n\); check endpoints separately when k=0 or k=n. The parameter domain is part of the problem.

sections.title: Support comes before differentiation
sections.text: Using the density \(f(x;\theta)=\theta^{-1}\mathbf{1}\{0\le x\le\theta\}\), independent uniform observations have likelihood zero below their maximum M and \(\theta^{-n}\) for \(\theta\ge M\). The maximum is at M, even though there is no interior stationary point.

sections.title: Fit the center and the scale
sections.text: For iid normal data with nonzero empirical spread, maximizing over mean and positive variance yields \(\hat\mu=\bar x\) and \(\hat\sigma^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\). The n-1 correction targets unbiasedness instead. Identical observations give an unbounded density as variance approaches zero, not a positive-variance maximum.

sections.title: Evidence is not the same as row count
sections.text: Likelihood multiplication requires the stated independence or conditional-independence model. Duplicating a record does not create new observations. Curvature describes sensitivity within the assumed model; a misspecified or selected sample can still produce a sharply wrong answer.

sections.title: A new sampling rule changes the likelihood
sections.text: For independent exponential waits with rate \(\lambda>0\), fully observed waits contribute densities and right-censored waits contribute survival probabilities. If d events are observed over total exposure T, the likelihood is proportional to \(\lambda^d e^{-\lambda T}\), giving \(\hat\lambda=d/T\) when d>0.

lessons.example: For completed independent exponential waits of 1, 2, 3 and 4 seconds, total exposure is 10 seconds and the maximum likelihood rate is \(\frac{4}{10}\) = 0.4 per second. If instead only two events occur over the same total exposure and the rest is independently right-censored, the rate estimate is \(\frac{2}{10}\) = 0.2 per second. Exposure includes censored waiting time.
lessons.check: Ten independent Bernoulli trials share p, with seven successes. On 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, which statement is justified by maximum likelihood alone?
options: The MLE is 0.7, but this does not give a posterior probability for p.
The probability that p equals 0.7 is 70%.
The MLE is 0.5 because the parameter range is symmetric.
The likelihood is automatically a probability density over p.
lessons.explanation: The log-likelihood is maximized at k/n = 0.7. A posterior requires a prior and normalization; likelihood maximization alone assigns no probability to the parameter.
objectives: Distinguish probability, density, likelihood and posterior.
Derive an MLE and check support, boundaries and existence.
Write a likelihood that matches dependence and censoring rather than blindly multiplying rows.

lessons.title: Covariance is a matrix constraint
lessons.intro: A covariance matrix describes variation in every linear combination of variables. Its entries cannot be chosen independently: the whole matrix must represent a possible joint system.

sections.title: What the entries mean
sections.text:
Let X be a column vector of d random variables with finite second moments, and let mu be its mean vector. The covariance matrix is
\[\Sigma=E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T].\]
Entry (i,j) is the covariance of variables i and j. Diagonal entries are variances; off-diagonal entries describe joint movement. The matrix is symmetric because covariance is symmetric.

A correlation matrix divides each covariance by the corresponding two standard deviations, assuming those standard deviations are positive. Its diagonal entries are one. Standardisation removes units but does not remove constraints between entries.

sections.title: A portfolio is a linear combination
sections.text:
For a real weight vector w, the scalar \(w^TX\) is a weighted combination of the variables. Its variance is
\[\operatorname{Var}(w^TX)=w^T\Sigma w.\]
Since a variance cannot be negative, a valid covariance matrix must give a nonnegative quadratic form for EVERY weight vector. This property is called positive semidefiniteness, abbreviated PSD.

Positive definiteness is stronger: the quadratic form is strictly positive for every nonzero w. A covariance matrix may be merely semidefinite when some nonzero linear combination is constant. Perfectly duplicated variables supply a simple example.

sections.title: Eigenvalues describe variation along directions
sections.text:
A real symmetric matrix can be decomposed into orthogonal eigenvector directions. Along an eigenvector, its quadratic form scales with the corresponding eigenvalue. Consequently a symmetric matrix is PSD exactly when all eigenvalues are nonnegative.

For two standardised variables with correlation rho, the correlation matrix has eigenvalues 1+rho and 1-rho. Their nonnegativity yields the familiar bound minus one to one. In larger systems, checking each pair separately is not enough: a vector involving several variables may still have a negative proposed variance.

Tiny negative eigenvalues in an estimated matrix may arise from rounding, but a materially negative one is evidence of an invalid covariance construction. Diagnose estimation, missing-data conventions and scaling before using the matrix in an optimisation.

sections.title: Three correlations must fit together
sections.text:
For standardised variables X, Y and Z, write a=Corr(X,Y), b=Corr(Y,Z) and c=\(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Z)\). Their correlation matrix is
\[R=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&c\\a&1&b\\c&b&1\end{pmatrix}.\]
Its determinant is \(1+2abc-a^2-b^2-c^2\). PSD requires that determinant to be nonnegative, along with the other principal-minor conditions. For correlations a and b in the usual range, rearrangement yields
\[(c-ab)^2\leq(1-a^2)(1-b^2).\]
Thus c lies between \(ab-\sqrt{(1-a^2)(1-b^2)}\) and the corresponding plus expression. This is a joint feasibility bound; it is not obtained by checking c alone.

sections.title: Show that the correlation bound is attainable
sections.text:
Set a=b=0.8. The allowed c interval is 0.64 plus or minus 0.36, so its minimum is 0.28. Construct independent zero-mean variance-one variables Y and U and define
\[X=0.8Y+0.6U,\qquad Z=0.8Y-0.6U.\]
Both new variables have variance one. Their correlations with Y are 0.8, and their covariance with each other is 0.64-0.36=0.28. Because their variances are one, that covariance is also their correlation.

The boundary matrix is singular: X+Z=1.6Y exactly. Singularity here is a meaningful linear relationship, not a contradiction. A construction proves that the algebraic lower bound can actually occur.

sections.title: Why direct inversion can be fragile
sections.text:
An invertible covariance matrix can still be ill-conditioned: a tiny variance along one direction makes inverse-based weights extremely sensitive to estimation noise. Near-duplicate variables are a typical cause. A numerically returned inverse is not proof that the resulting estimate is stable.

When solving a linear system, prefer an appropriate solver or factorisation to explicitly forming an inverse. Cholesky factorisation is suited to symmetric positive-definite matrices; a singular PSD matrix may require an eigenvalue or singular-value treatment. Regularisation can improve stability but changes the problem, so explain what assumption or penalty it introduces.

Inspect both feasibility and sensitivity. An optimiser may exploit precisely the covariance directions you estimate least reliably.

sections.title: Explain the matrix constraint in plain language
sections.text:
In an interview, start from “every weighted combination must have a nonnegative variance”. Then show how that condition produces a pairwise bound, an eigenvalue condition or a determinant inequality in the specific example.

For two independent unbiased estimates of one parameter with variances v1 and v2, weights w and 1-w give variance w²v1+(1-w)²v2. Differentiation gives w=v2/(v1+v2): weights are proportional to inverse variances. At v1=1 and v2=4, weights are \(\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{5}\) and combined variance is \(\frac{4}{5}\). With covariance c, the derivative instead gives w=(v2-c)/(v1+v2-2c) when the denominator is positive and these weights are permitted. Boundaries or a zero denominator need separate treatment. Dependence changes the optimisation.

Avoid treating PSD as a magic property detached from random variables. Also avoid claiming every PSD matrix must be invertible: semidefinite includes zero eigenvalues. If you propose a matrix with unusual correlations, try a simple weight vector or explicit variable construction to check what it means. Feasibility and profitable predictive information are separate issues.

lessons.example: Suppose X and Y are standardised and perfectly correlated. Their covariance matrix has rows [1,1] and [1,1]. The variance of X-Y is zero, while the variance of X+Y is four. Its eigenvalues are zero and two, so it is valid PSD but singular. This example simultaneously explains why zero eigenvalues are allowed and why a formula requiring an ordinary inverse cannot be used without checking invertibility.

lessons.explanation: An eigenvector with negative eigenvalue would have negative portfolio variance.

lessons.title: Regression as projection
lessons.intro: Least squares is a geometric projection and an optimisation problem. Derive its algebraic properties, then separate those properties from causal and out-of-sample claims.

sections.title: Define the regression problem
sections.text:
Observe n responses and p features per observation. Put the responses in a column vector y and the features in a design matrix X. If you include an intercept, add a column of ones to X. A coefficient vector beta predicts \(X\beta\), and the residual vector is \(r=y-X\beta\).

Ordinary least squares chooses beta to minimise the sum of squared residuals, \(\|y-X\beta\|^2\). This is a finite-data optimisation statement. It does not assume the features cause the response or that the fitted relation will remain stable on new data.

sections.title: Differentiate to obtain the normal equations
sections.text:
Differentiating the squared-error objective with respect to beta gives \(-2X^T(y-X\beta)\). At a least-squares solution,
\[X^TX\hat\beta=X^Ty,\qquad X^Tr=0.\]
The residual is orthogonal to every design column. Geometrically, the fitted response is the projection of y onto the space spanned by those columns.

If X has full column rank, the coefficient solution is unique and can be written using the inverse of \(X^TX\). In practical numerical work, solve the system with a stable factorisation rather than explicitly computing that inverse. If columns are redundant, coefficients need not be unique even though the fitted projection is.

sections.title: Why residuals sum to zero with an intercept
sections.text:
The intercept column contains one in every row. Orthogonality to that column means \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_i=0\). Equivalently, differentiating the loss with respect to the intercept gives minus twice the residual sum, which must vanish at an optimum.

Without an intercept column, there is no normal equation requiring that sum to be zero. With penalised or constrained fitting, inspect the actual objective and constraints rather than importing every unconstrained OLS property automatically.

A zero average in-sample residual is an algebraic consequence of fitting the intercept. It does not establish an unbiased future forecast: a model can satisfy it on training data and systematically miss on a changed population.

sections.title: The population slope is a covariance ratio
sections.text:
For a population regression of Y on one nonconstant feature W with an intercept and finite second moments, minimising expected squared error gives
\[b=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(W,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(W)},\qquad a=E[Y]-bE[W].\]
One derivation centres both variables, expands the squared-error expectation and differentiates the quadratic in b. This population coefficient is different from the random estimate fitted on one sample.

The slope describes the best linear prediction under this squared-error criterion. Even if the actual conditional mean is nonlinear, the population linear projection still has a well-defined meaning under these moment assumptions.

sections.title: Measurement error in the feature
sections.text:
Suppose \(Y=\beta X+\epsilon\), but you observe \(W=X+u\). Assume X, u and epsilon are mutually independent, centred, with finite variances. Then \(\operatorname{Cov}(W,Y)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(X)\), while \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(u)\). Hence
\[b=\beta\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(u)}.\]
This shrinks the population slope toward zero. With beta=2, signal variance one and measurement-error variance three, the observed-feature slope is one half.

If u and epsilon are correlated, an additional covariance enters the numerator; attenuation can fail. Measurement error only in the response has a different consequence under independent, mean-zero error. State which variable is contaminated.

sections.title: Regularisation changes the objective
sections.text:
Ridge regression adds a penalty proportional to the squared coefficient norm, typically leaving the intercept unpenalised. For the penalised feature coefficients, the normal equations gain a positive diagonal term. This discourages large unstable coefficients and can reduce variance at the cost of bias.

Standardisation matters because a coefficient penalty depends on feature units. Fit scaling parameters on training data only, and apply those parameters to validation data. Regularisation strength is a selected model choice; evaluate that selection without using the final holdout.

Better numerical stability does not prove better deployment performance. Compare with a simple baseline under the same chronological validation and cost assumptions.

sections.title: Prediction, explanation and causation
sections.text:
An association may arise because a feature causes the response, the response affects the feature, or another variable affects both. OLS orthogonality by itself does not identify a causal effect. If important omitted factors correlate with included features, the slope can absorb their influence.

When asked to explain a fitted coefficient, state the population, information set, conditioning variables and target. When asked to defend a prediction, discuss availability, validation and distribution changes. A statistically precise in-sample coefficient can still be unusable in a real decision if its input was only available afterward.

lessons.example: Take centred independent X, u and epsilon, with variances one, three and any finite error variance, and let Y=2X+epsilon and \(W=X+u\). Compute covariance first: it is two because every cross covariance vanishes. Compute W's variance: one plus three equals four. The slope is \(\frac{2}{4}\)=0.5. Now introduce Cov(u,epsilon)=c while keeping the other required cross covariances zero: the slope becomes (2+c)/4. This shows exactly which independence assumption supported attenuation.

lessons.title: Inference is a procedure
lessons.intro: A statistical conclusion depends on a complete procedure: hypotheses, statistic, sampling plan and interpretation. A small p-value cannot compensate for changing those rules after looking at the data.

sections.title: Specify the question and hypotheses
sections.text:
A null hypothesis describes a population or data-generating model you want to assess; an alternative describes departures of interest. For example, a mean may equal zero under the null and differ from zero under a two-sided alternative. Choose the statistic and direction of extremeness before seeing the result.

A test statistic summarises the data. Its null distribution describes how that statistic varies when the null and the sampling assumptions hold. A test therefore depends on more than an observed number: sample selection, dependence, nuisance-parameter estimation and the stopping plan can all alter calibration.

sections.title: What a p-value conditions on
sections.text:
A p-value is the null-model probability of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed statistic, using the test's specified definition of extremeness. It conditions on the null model; it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true given your data.

A p-value of 0.03 does not supply a 97% posterior probability for the alternative. Posterior inference requires priors and likelihoods over the hypotheses. Nor does 0.03 measure economic importance or the chance a strategy will make money.

A valid level-alpha test rejects according to a rule whose type-I error is at most alpha under the relevant null assumptions. That long-run property belongs to the entire procedure.

sections.title: Confidence intervals and effect size
sections.text:
A 95% confidence-interval procedure covers the fixed target parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its calibration assumptions. The particular interval you observe is not assigned a 95% posterior probability for that fixed parameter by this frequentist interpretation.

For an iid Gaussian mean with known positive standard deviation sigma, an exact normal-based interval is \(\bar X\pm1.96\sigma/\sqrt n\) to the usual rounded quantile precision. With unknown variance, the iid Gaussian setting uses an appropriate Student-t quantile and sample standard deviation. Asymptotic approximations need their own conditions.

Report the estimate and its uncertainty together. A tiny but precisely measured effect may be statistically detectable and practically irrelevant after costs.

sections.title: Repeated looks change the test
sections.text:
Suppose you recompute an ordinary fixed-sample 5% test after each new observation and stop at the first rejection. You have changed the sampling plan from the one used to calibrate a single fixed-sample test. The probability of ever crossing a boundary can exceed 5%.

The sequential p-values are generally dependent, so treating every look as an independent test is another unsupported shortcut. The key issue is that the stopping rule creates repeated opportunities to reject, not that every conceivable stopping rule is invalid.

Two principled approaches are to precommit to the fixed sample size and test, or to use a sequential procedure with justified boundary/error control. Alpha-spending designs or appropriately constructed always-valid tests need their stated assumptions; naming a martingale alone is not a proof.

sections.title: Pooling can reverse comparisons
sections.text:
Consider an easy group and a hard group. In the easy group, treatment succeeds 9 out of 10 times and control 80 out of 100: treatment wins 90% to 80%. In the hard group, treatment succeeds 20 out of 100 and control 1 out of 10: treatment again wins, 20% to 10%.

Overall, treatment has 29 successes out of 110 and control has 81 out of 110. The pooled comparison reverses because the treatment population places much greater weight on the hard group. Different mixtures, rather than an arithmetic contradiction, create the reversal.

Before interpreting a pooled rate, ask whether group composition differs and what population-level effect you actually want to estimate.

sections.title: Adjustment requires a causal argument
sections.text:
Stratifying by a relevant common cause can help compare similar groups, but adjusting for every measured variable is not a universal solution. Conditioning on a collider, a variable influenced by both sides of a relationship, can create an association that was absent before conditioning. Unmeasured confounding can also remain.

Distinguish a descriptive comparison, a predictive model and a causal claim. Random assignment helps identify treatment effects under additional assumptions, but a retrospectively chosen subgroup can still suffer from selection. State why each adjustment variable belongs in the design rather than relying only on its predictive usefulness.

sections.title: Rehearse a defensible inference statement
sections.text:
A clear statement identifies the target, estimate, uncertainty method, sample construction and decision rule. Add whether the hypothesis was selected before or after exploring the data, and whether any repeated looks or multiple candidate tests occurred.

If a result loses significance after a valid design correction, explain what information the original calculation omitted. Do not replace a missing inference design with a confident narrative. In quant research, the statistical procedure and the chronology of information are both part of the evidence.

lessons.example: Take the two-group comparison above. Treatment's pooled success rate is \(\frac{29}{110}\), about 26.4%; control's is \(\frac{81}{110}\), about 73.6%. Yet treatment wins within both groups. Recompute the comparison using a common \(\frac{50}{50}\) mixture: treatment averages (90%+20%)/2=55%, while control averages (80%+10%)/2=45%. This arithmetic isolates the composition effect. It does not, by itself, prove that either mixture identifies a causal treatment effect.
lessons.check: Does \(p=0.03\) imply a 97% probability the alternative is true?
options: No; posterior inference needs priors and likelihoods
lessons.explanation: The two probabilities condition on different things.
objectives: Interpret p-values and confidence intervals correctly.
Identify the sampling procedure behind an error-rate claim.
Explain optional stopping and reversals after pooling.
