lessons.title: Dependent returns and effective sample size
lessons.intro: Time-series observations can carry repeated information. Derive how lagged covariance changes uncertainty before using iid standard errors or square-root-of-time scaling.

sections.title: Define the time-series assumptions
sections.text:
A time series records observations in order, such as X1, X2 and so on. Weak stationarity means the mean is constant, variances are finite and constant, and covariance depends only on the lag separating observations. It does not require independence or a Gaussian marginal distribution.

Write \(\gamma_h=\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t+h})\). The lag-zero value is the marginal variance. When it is positive, autocorrelation at lag h is \(\gamma_h/\gamma_0\). Stationarity concerns the population model; an apparently stable plot is not sufficient evidence for it.

sections.title: Count each lag's covariance contribution
sections.text:
For a stationary series of n observations, expand the variance of their sum. There are n variance terms. At lag h, there are n-h unordered observation pairs, each contributing covariance twice. Therefore,
\[\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{t=1}^nX_t\right)=n\gamma_0+2\sum_{h=1}^{n-1}(n-h)\gamma_h.\]
Divide by n squared to obtain mean-estimation variance. Equivalently,
\[\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)}{\gamma_0/n}=1+2\sum_{h=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac hn\right)\frac{\gamma_h}{\gamma_0}.\]
The taper 1-h/n counts fewer pairs at long lags. The iid formula discards every nonzero-lag term.

sections.title: The stationary AR(1) model
sections.text:
Consider \(X_t-\mu=\rho(X_{t-1}-\mu)+\epsilon_t\), with absolute rho less than one, independent centred innovations of variance tau squared, and the stationary solution. Then marginal variance is \(\tau^2/(1-\rho^2)\), and autocorrelation at lag h is rho to the power h.

The coefficient rho is not the innovation variance or the marginal variance. Positive rho produces persistence; negative rho produces alternating-sign autocorrelation. At absolute rho at least one, the usual stationary formulas no longer apply to this model.

If you initialise an AR(1) simulation at a fixed zero rather than its stationary distribution, its early observations do not automatically have stationary variance. Account for initialization or use an appropriate burn-in when the experiment requires stationarity.

sections.title: Large-sample variance inflation
sections.text:
For fixed absolute rho less than one and a long sample, the finite-lag taper becomes negligible in the AR(1) sum. The geometric series gives
\[1+2\sum_{h=1}^{\infty}\rho^h=\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}.\]
Thus mean-estimation variance is approximately marginal variance divided by n, multiplied by this factor. For rho=0.8, the factor is nine. The iid standard error understates the approximate standard error by a factor of three, because standard error is a square root.

Near a unit root, or in a short sample, the finite-n terms matter. The approximation assumes rho stays fixed as n grows; it should not be invoked blindly when persistence grows with sample size.

sections.title: Define effective sample size for a specific estimator
sections.text:
Define \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}\) by equating mean-estimation variance to \(\gamma_0/n_{\mathrm{eff}}\). The AR(1) asymptotic approximation becomes
\[n_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx n\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}.\]
For \(n=100\) and rho=0.8 it is \(\frac{100}{9}\), about 11.11. The exact finite-n tapered variance yields a somewhat different number, about 11.63. Specify which quantity the question requests.

This is an information comparison for estimating the mean, not a universal count of independent rows for every estimator. Negative autocorrelation can produce a value larger than n under this definition because alternating fluctuations reduce mean variance.

sections.title: Why square-root-of-time Sharpe scaling can fail
sections.text:
Suppose returns have constant per-period mean and stationary covariance. A k-period sum has expected return k times the per-period mean, but its variance includes the lag terms above. Multiplying a one-period Sharpe ratio by the square root of k assumes the summed-return variance grows exactly linearly in k, among other modelling conventions.

Positive serial covariance can make that scaling optimistic. Negative serial covariance can have the opposite effect. Compounded returns, changing exposure and nonstationarity add further distinctions. Derive the variance of the actual return object rather than applying an annualisation factor because it is familiar.

sections.title: Turn dependence into a validation question
sections.text:
Plot and estimate autocorrelation, but remember that estimates have sampling noise. Overlapping targets mechanically share future increments and can create dependence even when underlying single-period returns are independent. Repeated measurements of one common exposure can also inflate the apparent sample size.

A defensible explanation states the target estimator, dependence model, finite-sample formula or approximation, and how uncertainty was estimated. If the model is only a rough illustration, say so. Blocking, appropriate time-series standard errors and chronological validation address different aspects of dependence; none is an automatic cure for leakage.

lessons.example: For a stationary AR(1) mean with rho=0.8 and 100 observations, compare the asymptotic variance \(9\gamma_0/100\) with the iid variance \(\gamma_0/100\). The approximate standard-error ratio is three and the effective sample size is 11.11. For the exact comparison, sum \(1+2\sum_{h=1}^{99}(1-h/100)0.8^h\), approximately 8.6, giving \(\frac{100}{8.6}\), approximately 11.63. These two answers correspond to different approximations, not contradictory definitions.
lessons.check: With positive autocorrelation, the iid standard error of the mean is generally…
lessons.explanation: Positive covariance increases the variance of the mean.
objectives: Define weak stationarity, autocovariance and autocorrelation.
Derive exact mean-estimation variance and an AR(1) approximation.
State what effective sample size and Sharpe scaling do—and do not—mean.

lessons.title: Validation must imitate deployment
lessons.intro: Validation is a simulation of how a decision would have been made. Preserve the order of information, fit every transformation within that boundary, and separate model selection from final evidence.

sections.title: Start from the deployment question
sections.text:
Define the decision time, prediction target and horizon before splitting rows. If a model will be trained on past observations and used on later observations, a validation experiment should imitate that chronology. Randomly mixing past and future rows may answer an easier but irrelevant question.

A training set supplies information used to fit model parameters. A validation set supports choices such as feature sets or hyperparameters. A final test set assesses the procedure after those choices are fixed. These roles concern information flow, not the names assigned to three files.

Include the retraining schedule: a model fixed for a month differs from one refitted each day using newly matured labels.

sections.title: Walk forward through time
sections.text:
A walk-forward split trains on an earlier interval and evaluates on a later interval. An expanding window keeps all eligible historical data; a rolling window keeps a bounded recent interval. Choose that convention to match the proposed deployment and explain its tradeoff between sample size and changing conditions.

At a training cutoff, a row's features may exist but its future target may not yet be known. If a target uses the next five observations, the final five rows before the cutoff can have unfinished labels. Exclude them until those labels would have matured.

Record exact boundaries and whether endpoints are included. A chronological split with an incorrectly available target can still leak.

sections.title: Overlapping label intervals
sections.text:
Suppose the target for a sample beginning at time t uses outcomes through t+5. Adjacent samples share parts of their target intervals. A training sample whose target interval overlaps a validation target may reveal information about validation outcomes.

Purging removes training samples with label-information intervals that intersect the protected validation intervals under the chosen endpoint convention. The overlap rule should reflect what actually enters the label, not merely whether starting timestamps differ.

Draw a small timeline and mark both ends of every interval. For a validation sample using times 10 through 15, a training label using 8 through 13 shares future outcomes with it. A sample using only times 2 through 7 does not share that label interval, although other dependence can remain.

sections.title: Embargo needs a specific reason
sections.text:
An embargo excludes an additional neighbourhood around protected data to address information reuse or dependence beyond the label overlap rule. Its length should be justified by feature construction, publication delays, target horizons or the evaluation design.

An arbitrary percentage of rows is not a substitute for identifying the dependence. In a strictly past-to-future split, data after the validation interval are not used for that fold's training anyway; an after-validation embargo may add no protection there. Other cross-validation designs can reuse later samples, making that boundary relevant.

Purging, embargo and chronological ordering solve related but distinct problems. Explain which leak or dependence each step addresses.

sections.title: Transformations are part of fitting
sections.text:
A scaler, imputer, feature selector or learned representation uses data to choose parameters. Fit it using the training portion of each fold, then transform validation data using those fixed parameters. Fitting a scaler once on the full dataset gives the training procedure information about the validation distribution.

For example, a validation-period price jump changes the full-data mean and standard deviation. If the training feature scale already reflects that jump, the simulated historical training was not actually limited to what was known then.

A transformation using a fixed, genuinely pre-specified constant is different from one estimated from future rows. Distinguish their information sources rather than labelling every preprocessing operation alike.

sections.title: Selection belongs inside the evaluation loop
sections.text:
To evaluate a model-selection procedure, use chronological inner splits inside each outer training interval. Select hyperparameters on those inner splits, refit the selected configuration on the eligible outer training data and evaluate once on the outer validation interval.

If you choose the configuration with the best outer results, those outer intervals have become selection data. They cannot simultaneously remain untouched evidence for that selected configuration. An honest report states which choices each dataset influenced.

Reserve a final holdout for the frozen procedure. If a disappointing final result causes you to change the model, the accessed holdout is no longer an untouched final test for that new model.

sections.title: Validate the economic decision as well as the prediction
sections.text:
Specify how forecasts become positions or quotes, then evaluate executable prices after realistic information and order latency. Include fees, spread, impact, turnover and relevant constraints. A predictive metric and net performance can move in different directions.

Use the same information boundary and cost conventions for the baseline. A sophisticated model should not receive more favourable data or execution assumptions than a simple comparison.

Before presenting a result, trace one validation decision end to end: available features, fitted parameters, forecast, action, execution price and realised target. This audit often finds errors that aggregate metrics hide.

lessons.example: You train at time 100 on labels that use outcomes through five time units after each sample's start. A sample starting at 98 has a label ending at 103, so its target is not yet known at the training cutoff. A sample starting at 94 ends at 99 and may be eligible if all its inputs and target were available. Fit the scaler on eligible training rows only, choose parameters with earlier inner splits, and evaluate decisions after the cutoff using the frozen training state.
lessons.check: Where should a scaler be fitted during cross-validation?
lessons.explanation: Its fitted parameters are part of the model and cannot use the test fold.
objectives: Design chronological training and validation splits.
Identify overlapping targets and explain purging or embargo choices.
Keep transformation fitting, model selection and final evaluation separate.

lessons.title: Search size belongs in the result
lessons.intro: The best result in a large search is partly selected for favourable noise. Keep the size and structure of that search visible when interpreting a promising candidate.

sections.title: Start with the candidate population
sections.text:
Suppose only 2% of candidate ideas are genuinely useful under a stated definition. A screening test passes a useful idea with probability 90%, and passes a useless one with probability 10%. Sensitivity describes useful ideas; the false-positive rate describes useless ones. They are not probabilities of usefulness after observing a pass.

In 1000 candidates under these assumptions, expect 20 useful ideas, of which 18 pass, and 980 useless ideas, of which 98 pass. Among 116 expected passes, only 18 are useful. Thus
\[P(\text{useful}\mid\text{pass})=\frac{0.02\times0.9}{0.02\times0.9+0.98\times0.1}=\frac9{58}.\]
The approximately 15.5% posterior follows from the base rate as well as test performance.

sections.title: A second test is not automatically independent evidence
sections.text:
If two tests are conditionally independent GIVEN usefulness, their pass likelihoods multiply within each hypothesis. Two passes yield useful weight 0.02 times 0.9 squared and useless weight 0.98 times 0.1 squared, giving posterior \(\frac{81}{130}\), approximately 62.3%.

Conditional independence is doing substantive work. Two backtests on the same returns, with similar features and costs, may share the same noise or data error. Repeating the same test twice does not supply the likelihood multiplication above.

Specify why a new test measures something meaningfully different or uses appropriately held-out information. More result rows are not necessarily more independent evidence.

sections.title: Many null tests create more rejection opportunities
sections.text:
For m independent tests of true null hypotheses, each with exact false-rejection probability alpha, the probability that none rejects is \((1-\alpha)^m\). Therefore the chance of at least one false rejection is
\[1-(1-\alpha)^m.\]
Twenty independent 5% tests give approximately 64.2%, even though each individual test is correctly calibrated at 5%. This is a family-wise probability, not the expected fraction of false findings among all selected discoveries.

If tests are dependent, this exact formula changes. Dependence does not erase the selection issue; it changes the joint probability structure. State when the independence approximation is being used.

sections.title: The winning score is a selected statistic
sections.text:
Imagine testing many models with no true difference in expected performance. Their validation estimates vary because of sample noise. Selecting the highest estimate selects a model that benefited from positive noise in that particular sample, so its reported score tends to overstate its future performance.

The search includes manual changes: choosing a universe after inspecting results, trying different horizons, dropping an inconvenient period or revising transaction-cost assumptions. A search ledger should record these choices, not only the final hyperparameter grid.

A plausible economic story can help propose an idea, but writing the story after selection does not remove the score's selection bias.

sections.title: Corrections answer different questions
sections.text:
A family-wise-error procedure aims to limit the probability of one or more false rejections within a stated family. A false-discovery-rate procedure controls a different average property of the rejected set under its assumptions. Neither is interchangeable with “probability this particular strategy is useful”.

For example, a Bonferroni allocation tests each of m hypotheses at alpha/m and gives a family-wise bound by the union bound, without requiring independence. It can be conservative, and its relevance depends on what the family and decision rule actually are.

Research replication on genuinely new information addresses predictive stability, which is not identical to a multiple-testing correction. Use procedures whose targets match the claim you want to make.

sections.title: Design discovery and confirmation separately
sections.text:
Use exploratory data to generate hypotheses and choose a procedure. Freeze the target, feature construction, model-selection rules and evaluation metrics before confirmation. Chronological nested validation can estimate the whole selection procedure; a separately protected final holdout supplies an additional check.

Keep rejected ideas and simple baselines in the record. Report the number of trials you know about and acknowledge unrecorded manual exploration when it occurred. A result can remain interesting while its evidence is weaker than the largest plotted Sharpe suggests.

If confirmation fails, diagnose the failure. Quietly turning the holdout into another tuning set and continuing to label it “unseen” makes the reported evidence misleading.

sections.title: What to say in an interview
sections.text:
Explain a winning backtest as the outcome of both an economic hypothesis and a selection process. Identify where candidate generation occurred, which data chose the winner, and which data assessed the frozen procedure.

Then discuss dependence among trials, uncertainty in costs and sensitivity to deployment choices. Avoid giving an exact adjusted significance level when the actual search family is unknown. The strong answer makes the missing information explicit and proposes a design that can produce interpretable new evidence.

lessons.example: You ran twenty independent exact-level 5% tests under their true nulls. The chance of no false rejection is \(0.95^{20}\), approximately 0.3585. The chance of at least one is approximately 0.6415. If the tests all return the same decision because they are perfectly dependent copies, the family-wise probability is instead 5%. These contrasting cases show why search count alone cannot establish an exact correction without the joint structure.
lessons.check: What does selecting the best validation result tend to do?
options: Remove the need for a final test
lessons.explanation: The winning model is often one that benefited from favourable validation noise.
objectives: Combine base rates with test sensitivity and false-positive rates.
Compute a family-wise false-rejection probability under independence.
Separate discovery, selection and confirmation of a research idea.
optionLabels: Remove the need for a final test

lessons.title: Defend a research result
lessons.intro: A research defence should make one result traceable from its proposed mechanism to available information, executable decisions and out-of-sample evidence.

sections.title: Define a claim narrow enough to test
sections.text:
Begin with the universe, decision horizon and mechanism. For example, a temporary liquidity imbalance might predict a short-horizon movement under a specified market state. That is more testable than “machine learning predicts markets”. State what observation would weaken or contradict the mechanism.

Define the target and action separately. Predicting the next recorded trade price does not automatically tell you when to buy, at which price or for how long to hold. A research result should specify how a forecast becomes an executable decision, including a no-trade condition when the forecast does not cover costs or constraints.

sections.title: Describe the information set
sections.text:
For every input, state when it was created, published, received and usable. Include revisions, delayed feeds and asynchronous markets. A feature labelled with an old event time may still arrive too late for the decision.

Record the training interval and which labels had matured at each refit. If you evaluate after realistic latency, update the execution price rather than assuming the earlier displayed quote remains available.

Choose one decision and reconstruct it from raw records. If you cannot demonstrate that its inputs existed at that time, an attractive aggregate performance chart does not resolve the information-validity question.

sections.title: Choose a baseline that tests the real claim
sections.text:
Compare against a simple forecast and a simple decision rule. For next-price prediction, carrying forward the last price can already be highly accurate when prices change infrequently. High classification accuracy may mainly predict the large “no change” class.

Use metrics tied to the decision: calibration, conditional payoff, turnover and net performance, alongside the forecasting measure. Apply the same universe, timestamps, execution delays and costs to the baseline and the proposed model.

If the advanced model only wins under more favourable execution assumptions, the comparison does not identify a modelling improvement.

sections.title: Separate gross and net economics
sections.text:
Gross price movement is not the same as realised profit. A taker generally buys at ask and sells at bid; fees and impact add further deductions. A passive fill has a conditional selection process and an uncertain execution probability, which also require modelling.

As a toy example, buying at 100.05 and later selling at an executable bid of 100.10 gives gross profit 0.05 per unit. Fees of 0.01 on entry and exit leave 0.03, before additional impact. A chart of midpoint movement could show a larger gain than this actual route.

State units: price units, percentages, basis points and monetary profit should not be mixed. Report turnover because repeated small costs can dominate a small predictive advantage.

sections.title: Diagnose a result that stops working
sections.text:
First check implementation and data: timestamps, universe, missingness, labels, positions and reproducibility of the earlier result. Then inspect the selection process: how many models and evaluation choices were tried, and whether protected data influenced them.

Next examine distribution and market-state changes. Compare feature distributions, conditional outcomes and baseline performance across periods. Finally decompose gross versus net performance, fills, spreads, fees and impact.

These causes can coexist. A regime-change story should predict a diagnostic that can fail; it should not be used to bypass an unresolved code or leakage error.

sections.title: Report uncertainty and robustness
sections.text:
A point estimate needs an uncertainty method appropriate to dependence and selection. Break results into meaningful subperiods without treating every slice as another chance to select a flattering view. Test reasonable execution and parameter perturbations chosen for substantive reasons.

Capacity asks what happens when proposed order size grows relative to available liquidity; performance at negligible size may not scale. Risk asks about drawdowns, concentration and exposures, not just average profit.

An honest result separates observations from assumptions and acknowledges where the model lacks executable data or a validated fill process. Calling such evidence preliminary can make the argument clearer and more credible.

sections.title: A compact defence sequence
sections.text:
Rehearse the defence in this order: hypothesis and mechanism; available information; target and action; baseline; chronological validation; gross and net performance; uncertainty and constraints; the most important falsification test.

For each claim, identify the record, calculation or experiment supporting it. If the strongest evidence is a time-aware backtest, call it a backtest rather than a demonstrated live edge. The interview goal is to show that your reasoning survives concrete scrutiny, including a realistic account of what remains uncertain.

lessons.example: A forecast predicts that the next recorded trade price will remain at 100.00. It is accurate on many rows because trades are sparse and the last price is stale. At your decision time, the executable ask may already be 100.08 and the bid 100.06. Buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses 0.02 before fees, despite an apparently accurate prediction of the recorded last price. Rebuild the target and baseline around prices and information usable by the decision.
lessons.check: Which is strongest evidence of a tradable result?
options: A reproducible time-aware net backtest with executable prices and stated assumptions
lessons.explanation: It tests the actual decision and its economics, while remaining evidence rather than a guarantee.
objectives: Connect the hypothesis, timestamps, target and decision rule.
Distinguish forecast accuracy, gross performance and executable net results.
Diagnose implementation, selection, regime and cost failures with falsifiable checks.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo with variance reduction
lessons.intro: Monte Carlo estimates an expectation through sampling. Treat simulation error explicitly, then design dependence or a control variable to reduce that error without changing the target.

sections.title: Define the target and the estimator
sections.text:
Suppose you want theta=E[g(X)] under a specified distribution for X. Draw independent samples from that distribution and average their transformed values Yi=g(Xi). The Monte Carlo mean is unbiased when the expectation exists; its variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)/n\) when the variance is finite.

Simulation estimates the chosen model's expectation. It does not establish that the model describes a real market. Separate Monte Carlo error, numerical approximation and model misspecification when reporting a result.

Specify the distribution, random-generation method, sample size and function being evaluated. A reproducible seed helps recreate a run, but one seed is not evidence that the estimated expectation is accurate.

sections.title: Quantify simulation uncertainty
sections.text:
For independent finite-variance Yi, estimate the mean's standard error with their sample standard deviation divided by the square root of n. Approximate confidence intervals need an appropriate sampling approximation and can be unreliable for small samples or rare heavy-tailed payoffs.

To reduce standard error by a factor of two using independent sampling alone, you need roughly four times as many draws. This square-root rate motivates variance reduction.

If you generate dependent pairs, the independent units may be the pair averages, not the individual members. Estimate variance at the level of independent simulation units. Treating two deliberately correlated values as two independent observations gives the wrong error estimate.

sections.title: Antithetic variables preserve marginals
sections.text:
Let U be \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Then 1-U is also \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). For a target g(U), the pair average \(A=[g(U)+g(1-U)]/2\) has the same expectation as g(U). Its variance is
\[\operatorname{Var}(A)=\frac12\left[\operatorname{Var}(g(U))+\operatorname{Cov}(g(U),g(1-U))\right].\]
An average of two independent copies instead has variance one half of Var(g(U)). Thus antithetic pairing helps when the covariance is negative; it can hurt when the covariance is positive.

Compare equal function-evaluation budgets. One pair uses two evaluations. Across n independently generated pairs, average n pair averages and estimate their sampling error as independent units.

sections.title: Work through a squared-uniform example
sections.text:
Take g(U)=U squared. The mean is one third, because integrating u squared from zero to one gives one third. The second moment is one fifth, so variance is \(1/5-1/9=4/45\).

For the pair, the product moment is \(E[U^2(1-U)^2]=1/30\), giving covariance \(1/30-1/9=-7/90\). Hence pair-average variance is
\[\frac12\left(\frac4{45}-\frac7{90}\right)=\frac1{180}.\]
Two independent squared uniforms have average variance \(\frac{2}{45}\). The antithetic variance is eight times smaller for these same two function evaluations. The improvement comes from negative covariance, not from a generic rule that symmetric inputs always help.

sections.title: Control variates subtract predictable noise
sections.text:
Let Y be the target variable and X a related variable whose expectation is known exactly. For a fixed coefficient c, define \(Z=Y-c(X-E[X])\). The subtracted term has expectation zero, so E[Z]=\(\mathbb E[Y]\).

Expanding variance gives
\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)+c^2\operatorname{Var}(X)-2c\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).\]
If \(\operatorname{Var}(X)>0\), differentiating in c yields \(c^*=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)\). When both variances are positive, the resulting variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1-\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)^2)\).

A positive correlation leads to a positive coefficient; a negative correlation leads to a negative one. The control must have a known mean under the same sampling distribution.

sections.title: Estimating the coefficient changes the argument
sections.text:
The unbiasedness proof above treats c as fixed. If you estimate it from the same simulation data and then plug it into the final mean, its dependence on those data can complicate a finite-sample unbiasedness claim.

A simple design estimates c from an independent pilot sample, freezes it, and generates a new main sample. Conditional on the pilot, the main estimator remains unbiased under the stated model. Another option is a properly analysed sample-splitting or cross-fitting procedure.

The optimal theoretical coefficient is not a guarantee that a noisy estimated coefficient improves variance. A weak or badly estimated control can deliver little benefit; measure the error using the actual design.

sections.title: Explain which error you reduced
sections.text:
Variance reduction changes Monte Carlo precision for a fixed target and model. It does not reduce data leakage, transaction-cost uncertainty or systematic modelling error. Report both the estimator and the independent sampling unit used for its error estimate.

As a check, compare a small independent-sampling baseline against the reduced-variance estimator over reproducible independent replications. Agreement in their estimated means supports correct implementation; the spread across replications illustrates the variance change. A single unusually close result is not enough to establish that an estimator is better.

lessons.example: For Y=U squared and control X=U, the known control mean is one half. Cov(U,U squared)=\(\frac{1}{4}\)-\(\frac{1}{6}\)=\(\frac{1}{12}\), and Var(U)=\(\frac{1}{12}\), so the optimal coefficient is one. The adjusted observation is \(Z=U^2-U+1/2\), with mean one third and variance \(\frac{1}{180}\). It equals the squared-uniform antithetic pair average algebraically. Here the two techniques lead to the same random quantity, although evaluating the original function twice and using a simple control can have different computation costs.
lessons.check: When does an antithetic pair reduce variance relative to independent draws?
options: Whenever it uses the same seed
When the covariance of the pair is negative
Only when the function is linear
lessons.explanation: Negative covariance lowers the variance of the average.
objectives: State the target distribution and estimate a Monte Carlo standard error.
Derive an antithetic pair variance and compare equal simulation budgets.
Derive the optimal control coefficient and protect unbiasedness when estimating it.

When the covariance of the pair is negative

lessons.title: Algorithms for a research notebook
lessons.intro: Build research primitives around explicit invariants. Derive a stable streaming update, a linear-time window algorithm and a timestamp-safe join, then test their boundaries.

sections.title: Separate the contract from the algorithm
sections.text:
An algorithm should implement a clearly defined mapping from inputs to outputs. Specify whether inputs are sorted, which windows include the current observation, how ties are resolved and what empty inputs return.

A fast implementation of a different contract is not an improvement. Write a slow transparent reference for small datasets first. Then derive an invariant: a statement about the algorithm's state that is true initially and remains true after every update.

Keep complexity claims precise. Linear time after sorting does not imply linear time for the entire pipeline when the input arrives unsorted. Output memory and auxiliary working memory are also different quantities.

sections.title: Why naive variance can lose precision
sections.text:
The identity variance=mean of squares minus square of mean is mathematically correct. When data have a very large common offset and small variation, these two large floating-point quantities can nearly cancel, amplifying rounding error.

Welford's algorithm maintains the count n, running mean m and sum of squared deviations M2. Its updates use deviations from the changing mean, avoiding that direct subtraction of two enormous nearly equal totals.

This improves numerical behaviour in common cases; it does not make floating-point arithmetic exact. Confirm the required behaviour for nonfinite inputs and very large magnitudes rather than silently accepting every value.

sections.title: Welford updates, in order
sections.text:
When a new value x arrives, increase n by one. Let delta be x minus the OLD mean. Update the mean to \(m_{\mathrm{new}}=m_{\mathrm{old}}+\delta/n\). Then update
\[M_{2,\mathrm{new}}=M_{2,\mathrm{old}}+\delta(x-m_{\mathrm{new}}).\]
The second factor uses the new mean. After n values, M2 equals the sum of squared deviations from the current sample mean. Dividing by n gives the descriptive variance of these observed values; dividing by n-1 gives the usual unbiased iid population-variance estimate when n is at least two.

Initialize count zero and M2 zero; handle the first observation consistently. Do not divide by n-1 for a single observation.

sections.title: A monotone deque for sliding maxima
sections.text:
For a current-inclusive window of positive integer size w, output the maximum among indices i-w+1 through i whenever the window is complete. Store candidate INDICES in a deque, ordered by increasing index and decreasing value.

Before processing an output, remove front indices older than the window. Before appending the new index, remove back candidates with value no greater than the new value: they are smaller or equal and will expire no later, so they cannot be needed for a future maximum. The front then identifies the current maximum.

Using “no greater” keeps the most recent of equal-valued candidates. If the task requires the earliest maximum index rather than only its value, reconsider this tie rule.

sections.title: Why total deque work is linear
sections.text:
Each index enters the deque once. It leaves at most once, either by expiring from the front or by being dominated at the back. Across n observations, the total number of insertions and removals is therefore proportional to n, even if one update removes many candidates.

This is an amortised argument, not a claim that every individual update performs only one operation. Auxiliary space is at most the window size, excluding the output list.

For [4,2,5,1] with a current-inclusive window of two, full-window maxima are [4,5,5]. A lagged window excluding the current observation is a different contract; adjust eligibility and indexing accordingly.

sections.title: As-of joins and invariants
sections.text:
For sorted decision times and feature availability times, maintain a feature pointer and the latest eligible record. Advance while the next feature is available at or before the decision under the stated tie convention. The invariant is that no unprocessed feature is eligible and the selected record is the most recent eligible one.

If timestamps repeat, define a stable secondary order or aggregate policy. If no feature has yet become eligible, emit the specified missing result. Event time alone is insufficient when availability differs.

A two-pointer scan takes linear time in the total records once inputs are sorted. Keep any sorting and data-cleaning cost separate in the analysis.

sections.title: Tests that probe the reasoning
sections.text:
For Welford, test constant values, a single observation and a large shared offset with small differences. For the deque, test increasing and decreasing sequences, equal values, window one and an input shorter than the window. For joins, test delayed availability, exact ties and a decision before the first feature.

Compare small random cases to a transparent reference and assert structural invariants. A correct result on one visible example does not establish the complexity argument; the insertion/removal reasoning does. In an interview, explain both why the state is sufficient and how its work is bounded.

lessons.example: Process [2,4,6] with Welford. After two values, n=2, mean=3 and M2=2. For x=6, delta=3, the new mean is four and the M2 increment is 3 times (6-4)=6. Final M2 is eight. Descriptive variance is \(\frac{8}{3}\); the usual sample variance is 8/(3-1)=4. Both values are legitimate answers to different variance definitions, so state the denominator convention before coding.

lessons.title: Fair value before a trade
lessons.intro: Calculate the value of the payoff under your current information, then compare it with the price you can actually trade. A fair-value estimate and a profitable execution are different objects.

sections.title: Define the contract and information
sections.text:
A contract specifies what you receive or owe under each future outcome. Let V denote its eventual cash payoff and let I denote the information currently available. In a simple risk-neutral, zero-interest, frictionless model, its fair value is the conditional expectation E[V|I]. This is a modelling assumption, not a universal pricing law for every risky asset.

Specify the settlement rule, currency, time horizon and information before calculating. If a payoff is the sum of three independent fair six-sided dice, each die has mean (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5. Before any reveal, expected payoff is 10.5.

Independence is not needed to add expectations. It is needed if you assert that revealing one die leaves the distributions of the others unchanged.

sections.title: A reveal changes the calculation
sections.text:
Suppose the first die is revealed as six and the remaining two are independent fair dice. The conditional expected payoff is now 6+3.5+3.5=13. The old value 10.5 used a different information set.

A noisy signal requires a probability-weighted update rather than replacing an unknown quantity with the signal itself. For possible values v and a signal s, compute posterior probabilities using prior weights times signal likelihoods, then calculate
\[E[V\mid s]=\sum_v vP(V=v\mid s).\]
A confident-looking observation cannot bypass the prior and observation model. Also distinguish seeing a value from seeing someone choose to trade: the latter may reveal information indirectly.

sections.title: Read a two-sided quote
sections.text:
A dealer's bid is the price at which the dealer buys from you; its ask is the price at which the dealer sells to you. If you take liquidity, you BUY at the ask and SELL at the bid. A quote 11 / 13 therefore offers you a purchase at 13 or a sale at 11.

The midpoint is 12 and the spread is two. The midpoint is a description of the quote, not automatically the contract's fair value. Your valuation could differ because of information, model assumptions or financing.

Describe the side explicitly in an interview. “Buy at the bid” would require posting an order and waiting for a fill, which is a different execution model from immediately accepting the displayed quote.

sections.title: Expected edge uses executable prices
sections.text:
For an immediate one-unit purchase held to settlement, expected profit before financing is fair value minus ask minus the applicable costs. For a permitted one-unit sale, it is bid minus fair value minus costs. Here costs should include the actual fees and other expenses of the assumed transaction.

With value 12 and quote 11 / 13, buying has edge -1 and selling also has edge -1 before costs. Neither is attractive under this objective. With value 13 and ask 12, the purchase has one unit of expected gross edge, which costs may reduce or eliminate.

If you plan to exit early, the relevant payoff is the executable exit value, not necessarily terminal settlement. Do not subtract a spread twice if your entry and exit prices already incorporate it.

sections.title: Expectations do not describe all the risk
sections.text:
A fair value can be correct while the realised payoff is very different. Before the dice reveal, the payoff ranges from three to eighteen; a buyer at 10.5 can lose or gain. Expected profit averages across repeated outcomes rather than promising each transaction's result.

An uncertain valuation adds another layer. Ask how edge changes under plausible posterior or parameter errors, and which losses are possible. If trades share the same underlying uncertain event, repeating them does not create independent trials.

A positive mean therefore does not settle whether a trade is feasible under a capital limit, acceptable under a risk objective or available in the stated size.

sections.title: Discounting and replication are distinct arguments
sections.text:
If a known cash payment K arrives after time T and the constant continuously compounded risk-free rate is r, its present value in the idealised borrowing/lending model is \(Ke^{-rT}\). A deterministic payment can be replicated by an appropriate investment in cash.

For uncertain payoffs, simply discounting a physical expectation is not generally enough to establish a no-arbitrage price. Replication or an appropriate pricing model may be required. Our dice examples deliberately use immediate settlement, risk-neutral valuation and no financing to isolate conditional expectation.

State these simplifying assumptions rather than applying the dice pricing rule to every derivative or risky security.

sections.title: Evaluate the information at execution
sections.text:
A quote can be chosen before the counterparty decides whether to trade. If their decision depends on private information, the distribution conditional on a fill differs from the prior distribution. Selling above prior fair value can then lose on average among actual sales.

A disciplined sequence is: define the payoff; identify the information; update the value; read the executable side; subtract costs; inspect risk; and ask what the fill itself reveals. The next module develops this final step with a complete probability tree. Keeping these objects separate makes both your arithmetic and your interview explanation easier to audit.

lessons.example: Three independent fair dice settle their sum. After seeing the first die as six, fair value is 13. A dealer quotes 12 / 14. Buying at 14 loses one unit in expectation; selling at 12 also loses one. Now suppose a different executable ask is 12.5 and the all-in purchase cost is 0.2. Expected net profit from buying and holding to immediate settlement is 13-12.5-0.2=0.3. This conclusion uses independent unrevealed dice and an uninformed fill; it does not say the payoff cannot fall below your purchase price.
lessons.check: Fair value is 12; bid is 11 and ask 13. Which trade has positive expected edge before costs?
lessons.explanation: Both directions lose one unit in expectation.
objectives: Translate a payoff into a conditional expected value.
Read bid and ask from the correct side of the trade.

lessons.title: Order flow is information
lessons.intro: An order is an observation about the person choosing to trade. Build the distribution of actual fills before deciding whether a spread protects you.

sections.title: Specify who trades and when
sections.text:
Consider a contract whose payoff V is either zero or 100, each with probability one half. A potential buyer's type is independent of V: with probability one half they are informed and observe V; otherwise they are uninformed.

For this particular model, an informed buyer buys only when V=100, while an uninformed buyer ALWAYS buys. Assume a displayed ask of 55, one-unit trades and no other costs. The unconditional expected payoff is 50.

The uninformed decision rule matters. Replacing “always buys” with “randomly buys or sells” changes the posterior. Write the actual rules before drawing a probability tree; a remembered answer from a similar example may be wrong.

sections.title: Enumerate the four branches
sections.text:
There are four equally likely combinations, each with probability one quarter: high value/informed, high value/uninformed, low value/informed and low value/uninformed. The first, second and fourth produce a buy. Low value/informed produces no buy.

Thus P(buy)=\(\frac{3}{4}\) and P(V=100 and buy)=\(\frac{1}{2}\). Bayes gives
\[P(V=100\mid\text{buy})=\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\frac23.\]
The payoff conditional on a buy is therefore \(100\times2/3=200/3\), about 66.67. Conditioning has removed the low-value informed branch and renormalised the remaining probability mass.

sections.title: Evaluate profit among actual sales
sections.text:
The dealer receives 55 upon a sale and ultimately pays V. Expected profit conditional on a buy is
\[E[55-V\mid\text{buy}]=55-\frac{200}{3}=-\frac{35}{3}.\]
That is an expected loss of approximately 11.67 per filled sale, despite asking five above the PRIOR fair value of 50. The execution selected a more valuable population of contracts.

Per opportunity, expected profit also includes the chance of no trade: (\(\frac{3}{4}\))(-\(\frac{35}{3}\))=-\(\frac{35}{4}\)=-8.75. Equivalently, weight the three filled branches' profits -45, -45 and 55 by one quarter each. Distinguish per-fill and per-opportunity quantities.

sections.title: A conditional break-even price needs its model
sections.text:
Holding the stated buying rules fixed, an ask of \(\frac{200}{3}\) would break even among fills before costs. But changing a quote can change who chooses to trade. In a realistic response model, conditional value depends on the quote as well as the observed side.

For example, an uninformed buyer may stop buying at a higher ask. Removing their low-value buys can increase adverse selection among remaining fills. One cannot generally solve for a profitable quote by taking a posterior calculated at one price and treating it as price-invariant.

The calculation above explains a mechanism under specified behaviour. An optimal quote requires a demand or arrival model, cost assumptions, position constraints and an objective.

sections.title: Inventory changes the objective
sections.text:
Inventory is the position you already hold. A dealer with positive inventory is long: it benefits from an increase in value and loses from a decrease. Even an informationally fair new purchase could increase exposure beyond a desired limit.

Adverse selection concerns what an incoming order reveals about value; inventory risk concerns the consequences of your existing and resulting position. They may interact, but they are not the same cost.

Track how a fill changes both belief and quantity. A customer's buy reduces the dealer's long inventory by one; a customer's sale to the dealer increases it by one. This sign convention helps prevent quote-skew arguments from being reversed.

sections.title: Quote centre and width have different effects
sections.text:
Under ordinary price-responsive flow, lowering both bid and ask can encourage customers to buy from a long dealer by offering a cheaper ask, while discouraging customers from selling to it by offering a less attractive bid. This shifts the quote centre downward.

Widening symmetrically lowers the bid and raises the ask. It can reduce fills on both sides, including the sales that would reduce a long inventory. It is therefore not the same action as changing the centre.

These are directional arguments under stated customer responses. Their magnitudes and even applicability depend on the market and flow model. There is no universal optimal skew amount supplied by the sign of inventory alone.

sections.title: Explain the mechanism with a counterexample
sections.text:
If informed and uninformed customers had identical trading behaviour independent of V, observing a buy would carry no information about V and conditional fair value would remain 50. If informed traders were much more prevalent, the posterior would move more sharply toward high value.

An interview defence should identify the exact branch that gets selected out, compute the conditional denominator, evaluate dealer profit and describe how changed behaviour would change the result. Do not replace this argument with “market makers earn the spread”: a spread can compensate for costs, but its existence does not prove positive expected profit.

lessons.example: Let the informed fraction be a, independent of payoff, with 0≤a≤1. Retain the rule that uninformed buyers always buy. A buy occurs with probability a/2+(1-a)=1-a/2, while high value AND a buy has probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Conditional expected payoff is 100/(2-a). It is 50 when a=0, \(\frac{200}{3}\) when a=\(\frac{1}{2}\) and 100 when a=1. More informed flow increases conditional value among sales. This formula relies on the same trading rules at every a; it does not establish how demand responds to a changed ask.

lessons.title: Continuation value and log growth
lessons.intro: Compare the payoff you can keep with the value of the remaining choices. Then see why maximising an expected payoff and maximising expected log wealth produce different decisions.

sections.title: Define the decision and objective
sections.text:
A fair six-sided die is rolled. After observing its value x, you may keep x or reroll once, accepting the second result. Assume no reroll cost, independent rolls, and an objective of maximising expected numerical payoff.

The expected payoff of a fresh roll is 3.5. After observing x, that number is the continuation value of rerolling: it averages the outcomes of your remaining action. Keep x if x exceeds 3.5 and reroll if x is smaller. For integer faces this means keep four, five and six.

The possibility of rolling six does not make rerolling a four optimal. You must compare a certain four with the entire distribution of the alternative, using the specified objective.

sections.title: Average the optimal conditional decisions
sections.text:
Before the first roll, each face occurs with probability one sixth. Optimal conditional values are 3.5 for initial one, two or three, and four, five or six for the other faces. Therefore
\[E[\text{optimal payoff}]=\frac{3(3.5)+4+5+6}{6}=4.25.\]
This is the value of the option to reroll selectively. Rerolling every face would give only 3.5; keeping every face also gives 3.5.

If a reroll costs one payoff unit, continuation becomes 2.5, so keep three through six. The ex-ante optimal value becomes (2×2.5+3+4+5+6)/6=\(\frac{23}{6}\). The action threshold changes because the alternative changed.

sections.title: More stages require backward induction
sections.text:
Let c_k be the value of a fresh roll when you may still reroll up to k times after observing it. With no rerolls, c_0=3.5. A new roll with k≥1 has value
\[c_k=\frac16\sum_{x=1}^6\max(x,c_{k-1}).\]
The previous-stage value is the continuation alternative. Thus c_1=4.25. With two rerolls available, keep five or six and reroll one through four, giving c_2=(4×4.25+5+6)/6=\(\frac{14}{3}\).

This finite-horizon recurrence uses independence and no costs. A different payoff utility, state-dependent cost or dependent roll process needs different states or continuation values. Name the remaining choices before applying a threshold.

sections.title: A good decision can lose this time
sections.text:
Keeping four is optimal in the one-free-reroll game even if a hypothetical reroll would have produced six. That unseen favourable outcome does not change the expected value at the decision point. Conversely, a poor decision can happen to pay off.

Distinguish policy quality, evaluated under the available information and objective, from the realised result. In research, comparing policies requires consistent information and sampling rules; selecting only lucky realised choices distorts the evaluation.

The objective itself matters. A person who strongly dislikes low outcomes may maximise expected utility rather than expected payoff, changing the continuation comparison.

sections.title: Set up the log-wealth model
sections.text:
Consider a repeated even-money bet with known win probability p, where \(0<p<1\). Assume independent rounds, a constant fraction f of current wealth staked each round, no fees, and 0≤f<1. A win multiplies wealth by 1+f; a loss multiplies it by 1-f.

Expected log growth per round is
\[g(f)=p\log(1+f)+(1-p)\log(1-f).\]
Logs convert multiplication of wealth into addition across rounds. This objective differs from expected profit in one round. Betting everything has a possible ruin outcome when \(p<1\) and makes log wealth undefined there, which is why f=1 is excluded.

sections.title: Differentiate and check the constraints
sections.text:
The derivative is \(g'(f)=p/(1+f)-(1-p)/(1-f)\). Setting it to zero gives p(1-f)=(1-p)(1+f), hence f=2p-1. The second derivative is negative throughout the domain, so the function is strictly concave.

With the long-only constraint 0≤f<1, the optimum is max(0,2p-1). At p=0.6 it is 0.2. Substitution gives 0.6 log(1.2)+0.4 log(0.8), about 0.0201 per round in the specified model.

If negative fractions were allowed, the feasible set and interpretation would differ. Derive the stationary point, then check the boundary and permitted actions; a formula without its domain is incomplete.

sections.title: Uncertain probabilities are a different problem
sections.text:
The derivation assumes p is known and the only payoffs are equal-sized wins and losses. An estimate of p from a short sample is uncertain; correlated opportunities, unequal payoffs, fees, liquidity constraints and larger-than-modelled losses also alter the objective.

A sensitivity calculation already shows fragility: changing p from 0.60 to 0.52 changes the toy optimum from 0.20 to 0.04. A model-based fraction cannot be carried directly into real trading without defining those missing features and constraints.

For an interview, present log growth as a mathematical decision model, derive it and explain its limitations. Do not confuse positive expected payoff with a license to increase size indefinitely.

lessons.example: At p=0.6, an even-money fraction \(f=0.2\) gives expected log growth about 0.0201. At f=0.5 it becomes 0.6 log(1.5)+0.4 log(0.5), about -0.03398, even though expected one-round wealth gain is f(2p-1)>0 in both cases. The larger fraction wins on average in the arithmetic one-round objective yet loses in expected log growth. The difference comes from the objective's treatment of downside compounding, not from different win probabilities.

lessons.title: Risk lives in joint exposures
lessons.intro: Positions interact through their joint payoffs. Measure the combined exposure, then separate an estimated variance from the constraints and tail behaviour it leaves out.

sections.title: Specify weights, units and returns
sections.text:
Let R_1 and R_2 be returns measured over the same horizon, and let w_1 and w_2 be portfolio weights fixed before those returns occur. In a simple linear portfolio, return is R_p=w_1R_1+w_2R_2. State whether weights are capital fractions, notionals or position quantities; the units of the resulting payoff differ.

For weights summing to one, this describes a fully allocated simple-return portfolio under the stated linear model. Shorts and leverage can make weights negative or make total gross exposure exceed one.

Do not combine daily variance with hourly covariance, or return weights with cash-profit variances, without conversion. A precise horizon and unit convention comes before the formula.

sections.title: Expand the square to see covariance
sections.text:
For finite second moments, centre both returns around their means and square the weighted sum. Taking expectations gives
\[\operatorname{Var}(R_p)=w_1^2\sigma_1^2+w_2^2\sigma_2^2+2w_1w_2\operatorname{Cov}(R_1,R_2).\]
Here sigma_i is the standard deviation of asset i. Covariance equals rho times sigma_1 times sigma_2, where rho is their correlation and both standard deviations are positive.

The cross term is why two individually risky assets can offset each other, or reinforce the same risk. With more assets the formula becomes \(w^\top\Sigma w\), where Sigma is the joint covariance matrix, not a list of isolated variances.

sections.title: Work through an equal-weight pair
sections.text:
Suppose both assets have variance four, so each standard deviation is two, and their correlation is 0.5. Their covariance is 0.5×2×2=2. At weights one half each, portfolio variance is
\[\tfrac14(4)+\tfrac14(4)+2(\tfrac12)(\tfrac12)(2)=3.\]
The standard deviation is sqrt(3), not three. At correlation zero variance becomes two; at correlation minus one half it becomes one; at correlation one it becomes four.

These comparisons hold variances and weights fixed. Correlation changing together with volatility can produce a larger risk increase than this isolated calculation suggests.

sections.title: Diversification depends on shared causes
sections.text:
Two instruments with different names may load on the same interest-rate, volatility or market factor. A schematic model R_i=beta_i F+epsilon_i separates a common factor F from residual components. Under uncorrelated factor and residuals, the portfolio's factor contribution is (sum of w_i beta_i)F.

Adding more positions does not necessarily reduce that shared loading. If all beta_i have the same sign, the common exposure can persist while independent residual noise averages away.

Explain what economic or statistical event could make the positions move together. Historical pairwise correlation is a summary of past joint variation, not a promise that dependencies stay fixed during stress.

sections.title: Stress the inputs and constraints
sections.text:
A covariance estimate has sampling error and may change with the regime. Recalculate portfolio behaviour under larger volatilities, stronger positive correlations and concentrated common shocks. Check whether the assumed covariance matrix is mathematically valid: every weighted variance must be nonnegative.

A capital limit, exposure cap or liquidity requirement is a constraint on permitted actions, not just a term inside expected profit. A trade with positive expected edge may breach a limit or be impossible to exit at the assumed size.

Stress scenarios are explicit alternatives, not forecasts with automatically known probabilities. Report which inputs moved, what stayed fixed and which constraint becomes binding.

sections.title: Variance does not specify the tail
sections.text:
Two payoff distributions can have the same mean and variance but different probabilities of severe loss. A normal approximation may miss jumps or a mixture with rare large negative outcomes. State the distributional assumption before turning a standard deviation into a tail-loss probability.

Even a numerical quantile does not describe how bad losses beyond it can be. Liquidity can also disappear in precisely the state when reducing exposure is most valuable.

Ask about downside magnitude, timing, financing and feasible exits separately. No single variance estimate answers every risk question, and a narrow confidence interval for a mean does not guarantee a harmless payoff distribution.

sections.title: Hedges leave model and nonlinear risk
sections.text:
Offsetting a linear factor loading can reduce first-order exposure, but estimated hedge coefficients can be wrong and change over time. Nonlinear instruments also have curvature and sensitivity to other state variables.

A delta-neutral option position, for example, removes a local first derivative with respect to the underlying at the current state. It can retain gamma, volatility and time exposure. A hedge that is neutral now may not remain so after a price move.

A strong interview answer computes the specified combined risk, identifies what the model omits and tests the conclusion under changed assumptions. It does not call a portfolio safe merely because it contains many positions or has a positive mean.

lessons.example: For the equal-weight, variance-four pair, covariance two gives variance three. If correlation rises from 0.5 to one while individual standard deviations also rise from two to three, the new covariance is nine and the portfolio variance is (\(\frac{1}{4}\))9+(\(\frac{1}{4}\))9+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))9=9. Standard deviation rises from sqrt(3) to three. Merely changing correlation at the old volatility would have predicted variance four and understated this joint stress. This is a scenario calculation, not an estimated probability that the scenario will occur.

lessons.title: The small mathematical-finance core
lessons.intro: Use payoff identities and local derivatives to understand the mathematical-finance essentials. Keep exercise style, financing and the meaning of each sensitivity explicit.

sections.title: Write the terminal payoff first
sections.text:
A European call with strike K and maturity T pays max(S_T-K,0), where S_T is the underlying price at maturity. A European put with the same strike and maturity pays max(K-S_T,0). European exercise means the payoff is determined at maturity; early exercise is not an available action.

Subtracting put payoff from call payoff gives S_T-K in both cases: if S_T≥K, the call contributes S_T-K and the put zero; if S_T<K, the call is zero and subtracting the put gives -(K-S_T).

This identity is exact at maturity. It is not an approximation and does not require knowing a volatility or a probability distribution.

sections.title: Replicate the difference today
sections.text:
Assume a non-dividend-paying underlying, a constant continuously compounded risk-free rate r, and frictionless trading with borrowing, lending and shorting available. Holding one unit of underlying and borrowing \(Ke^{-rT}\) today produces terminal value S_T-K, because the debt grows to K.

The call-minus-put portfolio has the same terminal payoff, so no-arbitrage implies
\[C-P=S_0-Ke^{-rT}.\]
Here C and P are current option prices and S_0 is the current underlying price. If equal payoffs had different prices under these assumptions, buying the cheaper portfolio and selling the more expensive one would create a price discrepancy with offsetting terminal payoffs.

Costs and trading constraints can prevent the idealised arbitrage trade. State them before interpreting a small observed discrepancy.

sections.title: Check the assumptions and direction
sections.text:
At S_0=100, \(K=100\) and \(r=0\), parity gives C-P=0. It states that call and put prices are equal for this setup, not that both options cost zero. Each can have positive value because its payoff is nonnegative and uncertain.

A known dividend changes the underlying replication's cash flows. American exercise introduces an early-exercise right, so the same European equality cannot simply be reused. Different strikes or maturities also destroy the matched payoff identity.

For an interview, derive the two terminal cases first. Then identify the portfolio replicating their difference and discount the deterministic debt. This is more robust than recalling a formula with an uncertain sign.

sections.title: Define local sensitivities
sections.text:
Let V(S,t) be the current value of a smooth instrument as a function of underlying price S and calendar time t, holding other model inputs fixed. Define delta as \(\Delta=\partial V/\partial S\), gamma as \(\Gamma=\partial^2V/\partial S^2\), and theta as \(\Theta=\partial V/\partial t\).

Delta describes the local linear response to price. Gamma describes the change in that slope as price changes. Theta describes the response to passing calendar time with the other inputs held fixed.

If a model instead uses time remaining tau=T-t, its derivative with respect to tau has the opposite sign to calendar-time theta. Specify which clock you differentiate before assigning a sign.

sections.title: Use a Taylor expansion carefully
sections.text:
For small changes, a common approximation keeps second order in price and first order in time:
\[\delta V\approx\Delta\,\delta S+\tfrac12\Gamma(\delta S)^2+\Theta\,\delta t.\]
This deliberately drops higher price terms, time curvature and cross terms. It is not an exact full second-order expansion in every variable. Volatility and rate changes require additional sensitivities when they occur.

At delta zero, gamma 0.08 and a price move of five, with no time or other input change, the retained gamma term is (\(\frac{1}{2}\))×0.08×25=1. Reversing the sign of the price move leaves that term unchanged because it is squared.

sections.title: Neutrality is local and variable-specific
sections.text:
Delta-neutral means the combined first derivative with respect to S is zero at the current state. It does not make gamma zero, remove time exposure or fix the response to volatility. After S changes, delta itself generally changes approximately by gamma times the price move.

A finite move can also make the Taylor approximation inaccurate, especially near a discontinuity or when omitted derivatives are large. Compare with full model repricing when available, and identify the step size over which the approximation is reasonable.

Greeks depend on the pricing model and its state inputs. A derivative calculated correctly inside a misspecified model can still misdescribe realised exposure.

sections.title: Check units, net positions and payoff logic
sections.text:
For an option value measured in currency and an underlying price in currency per unit, delta has units of underlying quantity, and gamma has units that make gamma times squared price change a currency amount. Theta must match the time unit: a per-year theta cannot be multiplied directly by a number of days.

Sum sensitivities across positions with their signed quantities before calling the portfolio neutral. Buying and selling identical contracts offset exposures; different strikes or maturities can offset one derivative while retaining others.

The small core is payoff replication plus explicit local approximations. These tools help you reason about a changed contract or assumption without memorising product trivia.

lessons.example: Suppose a portfolio has delta 0.4, gamma 0.08 and theta -0.2 per day. For an underlying increase of five over one day, holding other inputs fixed, the retained approximation is 0.4×5+(\(\frac{1}{2}\))×0.08×25-0.2×1=2.8. For a decrease of five it is -2+1-0.2=-1.2. The gamma contribution is one in both directions; the delta contribution changes sign. These are approximate value changes using sensitivities at the initial state, not guaranteed realised profits.

lessons.title: Strategic inference and calibration
lessons.intro: Condition on the other side’s decision, and evaluate forecasts with a loss that matches the task. Winning, confidence and numerical precision can each hide a selection problem.

sections.title: Common value and private value differ
sections.text:
In a common-value auction, the eventual object value V is shared across bidders but initially uncertain. Each bidder receives a noisy private signal about it. The highest estimate can win partly because it contains an unusually favourable error.

In a private-value model, bidders instead have their own values for the object. Other bidders' low valuations do not necessarily mean your own consumption value is low. Strategic bidding still matters, but the information problem differs.

Specify which model applies, what signals reveal, how bids relate to signals, and the auction format. There is no single correct bid formula for every auction or every noisy estimate.

sections.title: Winning is an additional observation
sections.text:
Suppose m≥2 bidders observe signals s_i=V+epsilon_i, where the noises are independent of V and of each other, have a continuous cumulative distribution F, and higher signals lead to higher bids. Ignore reserves and ties. Conditional on your signal s and value v, you win when all other noises are below s-v.

Consequently,
\[P(\text{win}\mid V=v,s_i=s)=F(s-v)^{m-1}.\]
For a fixed s, this likelihood decreases as v increases. A high true value would make the other bidders' signals high too, making it less likely that your observed s beats all of them.

Conditioning on your signal alone omits this information from the winning event.

sections.title: Write the posterior correction
sections.text:
When the prior and noise have densities, the posterior after observing signal s and winning is proportional to
\[f_V(v)f_\varepsilon(s-v)F(s-v)^{m-1}.\]
The first two factors describe inference from your signal alone. The extra winning factor gives relatively more weight to smaller common values under this model. Normalise the product before taking its expected value.

This explains the winner's-curse correction: evaluate value conditional on both your signal and winning, rather than bidding from the signal-only estimate. It does not by itself solve strategic equilibrium bidding. Payment rules, competitors' strategies and your objective are additional parts of that problem.

sections.title: Forecast probabilities rather than certainty
sections.text:
A probability forecast p describes an uncertain binary outcome Y∈{0,1}. A forecast of 0.7 does not mean each event will succeed or that an observed failure proves the forecast wrong. Over many comparable events with that forecast, a calibrated forecaster should see a success rate near 0.7, allowing for sampling variability.

Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed frequencies. It is different from sharpness: how much forecasts vary away from the base rate. A constant base-rate forecast may be calibrated while failing to distinguish easier from harder cases.

Assess groups of forecasts with sufficient data, a defined population and honest evaluation timestamps. Repeated outcomes about the same event do not create independent calibration observations.

sections.title: Derive the Brier score
sections.text:
For one binary outcome, the Brier loss is (p-Y)². For n forecasts, the score is their average loss; lower is better. If the true conditional success probability is q, expected loss is
\[q(1-p)^2+(1-q)p^2=(p-q)^2+q(1-q).\]
The second term is irreducible uncertainty at that information set. The first is minimised by reporting p=q. Thus this loss rewards an honest probability under the model rather than an artificially confident zero or one.

This expectation result does not say the honest forecast beats every other forecast on every realised event. A single realised outcome can make an overconfident lucky prediction look better.

sections.title: Evaluate out of sample with the right context
sections.text:
Suppose ten comparable forecasts are all 0.7 and seven outcomes succeed. Each success contributes 0.09 and each failure 0.49, so the average Brier score is (7×0.09+3×0.49)/10=0.21.

That group matches the advertised frequency exactly, but ten events are too few to establish precise long-run calibration. Compare with a meaningful base-rate forecast and evaluate on data not used to adjust probabilities. If the sample base rate is estimated from those same ten outcomes, recognise that this baseline used evaluation information.

A score aggregates performance. Inspect reliability by probability range and whether the forecasts distinguish subgroups without selecting favourable bins after looking at the outcomes.

sections.title: Use an error scale that matches the quantity
sections.text:
For a positive quantity y and positive estimate x, absolute log-ratio error |log(x/y)| treats multiplication by two and division by two symmetrically: both have error log(2). Ordinary absolute error gives very different penalties depending on the unit and magnitude.

This can suit order-of-magnitude estimates, but it is undefined at zero and penalises near-zero values strongly. Choose the loss because of the task, not because it makes a chosen estimate look good. A range with stated assumptions is often more informative than a highly precise unsupported number.

Across auctions and forecasts, the recurring discipline is the same: identify the information used, model how observations were selected and score the conclusion with an explicit objective.

lessons.example: For a binary common value V∈{0,100} with equal prior weights, imagine your signal has equal likelihood under both values. Before considering the win, your posterior is still one half each. Suppose the probability of winning conditional on that signal is 0.8 when V=0 and 0.2 when V=100. After winning, the unnormalised weights are 0.4 and 0.1, so the high-value posterior is \(\frac{0.1}{0.5}\)=0.2 and conditional expected value is 20. This deliberately specified likelihood example shows why a signal-only value of 50 can be too high. Computing an actual bid also requires the auction's payment and strategic rules.
